leads.title: Show HN: ApiClay – Turn a Website, Google Sheet or Database into a Paid API
leads.description: Hi HN, I’m a reverse engineer, and I’ve seen the same problem repeatedly: people need data, but the path from “I need this” to “my app, agent, or workflow can use it” is messy. Vibe coders want a working endpoint in minutes. Developers want clean docs, predictable JSON, and no surprise integration work. Businesses want to enrich lists, monitor changes, and safely expose internal data. AI agents need APIs they can discover and call reliably. Sometimes, the API simply doesn't exist. ApiClay makes that whole loop easier. You can search a catalogue of APIs and datasets, inspect them in a playground, and copy ready-to-run JavaScript, Python, or cURL snippets into your app. Each API has its own reference, pricing, trials, and usage terms, so you can see what you’re calling before you go live. But ApiClay is not just an API marketplace. If the API you need does not exist, you can create one with Website to API: give it a page, map the fields you care about, and publish a stable JSON endpoint. It works with static and JavaScript-heavy pages, and can return clean Markdown, JSON, text, or links. You can also turn what you already have into an API: * MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Google Sheets, Airtable, Excel/CSV, and HTTP services can become API endpoints. * Import an OpenAPI/Swagger file to get docs, a playground, and billing for an existing API. * Publish only the fields you choose, control access, set trials, plans, usage limits, and pricing. * Aggregate multiple providers into one tidy response for comparison-style products. For AI, ApiClay exposes an MCP endpoint so Claude, ChatGPT, or custom agents can search for an API, inspect it, and call it. The idea is simple: instead of an agent hallucinating a data source, it finds a real API and returns an answer backed by live data. There are also practical data tools beyond discovery: * Websets / enrichment: upload a list, enrich each row, set a spend cap, and export the result. * Monitors: watch an API or webpage and receive a signed webhook when something changes. * Cloud browser: automate a browser session for pages behind clicks or JavaScript rendering, then return the values your app needs. * Extraction: turn a page into clean Markdown, JSON, text, or links without maintaining your own scraper. For people publishing APIs, credentials stay encrypted on ApiClay and are not exposed to buyers; publishers control pricing, limits, trials, and access. For consumers, browsing and reading docs are free, while paid calls are charged per request and shown before use. *ApiClay is where you find the data API you need, build the one that is missing, let AI agents use it, and optionally sell it.* We’d love feedback from HN—especially from developers building data-heavy products, teams dealing with messy internal sources, and anyone experimenting with agent-driven workflows.

leads.description: About 3Y Health 3Y Health is building the operating system for healthcare practices, an AI-native platform that helps clinicians start, run and grow their practice. We work as a managed services organization (MSO): along with the software, our operations team runs the back office for the clinics we partner with, including billing, insurance and compliance. We currently serve applied behavior analysis (ABA) therapy practices and are expanding into speech, occupational and physical therapy, and psychiatry. About the role Members of Technical Staff own features end to end. You'll work with the clinicians and operators who use what we build, scope the problem, design and build the solution across the stack, deploy it and follow how it performs in production. Our engineering team is flat, with no sub-teams, so you'll work across the whole platform. We build with AI coding agents every day and expect you to do the same. What you'll do Design and build AI agents and automated workflows for clinic operations, such as insurance benefits verification, prior authorizations, patient intake, claims and clinical documentation Build features for clinicians, patients and families, and our internal operations team, on web and mobile Take ambiguous problems from 0 to 1, working with operators and clinicians to define the problem, write the spec and ship a first version Design the services, data models and APIs behind your features and manage the infrastructure as code Own your services in production: deployments, monitoring and incident response Write evals for model-facing features and track the metrics of the workflows you ship Work with protected health information (PHI) safely, with least-privilege access, no PHI in logs and auditable changes Build and maintain the skills, plugins, MCP integrations and review bots our engineers use with Claude Code and Codex Our stack Backend: Python (our primary language for new services), Kotlin with Hasura (GraphQL) on our established platform, plus TypeScript (NestJS) and some Go Frontend and mobile: React, Next.js, React Native Data: PostgreSQL (including pgvector), Snowflake Workflows and contracts: Temporal, gRPC/Protobuf Infrastructure: AWS (ECS Fargate, RDS), Terraform, GitHub Actions, Datadog, LaunchDarkly AI: Claude and OpenAI models, Claude Code and Codex, with our own skills, plugins, MCP integrations and an AI code-review bot Must-haves 5+ years of experience building and shipping production software Recent, hands-on experience using or building AI harnesses: the layer around a model or coding agent (project instructions, tools and MCP servers, skills, hooks, subagents, evals), not only calls to a model API. You can show what you set up or built. At least one personal project you built and published on the web, live and usable by anyone, ideally a SaaS with payments working (e.g. Stripe). Share the link when you apply. What we're looking for A track record of owning products or features end to end, from an unclear problem to a system people depend on Strong full-stack skills in Python and TypeScript, with experience across frontend, backend, databases and cloud infrastructure Comfort working in a large, established codebase Hands-on experience building with LLMs, including tool use, agent orchestration, structured outputs, retrieval and evals (LangGraph, an agents SDK or similar) Daily use of AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex or Cursor. You know how to set them up for a codebase (project instructions, skills, MCP servers, hooks, subagents), run several tasks in parallel and review their output carefully. If you haven't heard of Claude Code, this role is likely not a fit. Good product sense and the ability to make solid UI decisions without a dedicated designer, using our component library High agency: you unblock yourself, look for context and ask questions when you need to Clear written communication. The team is distributed across time zones and most decisions happen in specs, PRs

leads.title: Senior Security Engineer, AI Security
leads.description: Description Security Engineers at Dropbox safeguard our digital ecosystem alongside a diverse team of professionals dedicated to protecting our products and users. Trusted by millions, our mission is to integrate security seamlessly into Dropbox, empowering confident collaboration. In this role, you’ll help shape how Dropbox secures AI systems and agentic workflows, building and operating the controls that protect the infrastructure, tools, and data they rely on. You’ll tackle challenges such as prompt injection, secure agent access, and MCP integrations, turning emerging risks into practical, reusable safeguards. Partnering across engineering and security, you’ll lead hands-on work that enables teams to adopt AI safely while protecting customer data. Our Engineering Career Framework is viewable by anyone outside the company and describes what’s expected for our engineers at each of our career levels. Check out our blog post on this topic and more here . Responsibilities Design, deploy and operate infrastructure-level security controls for Dropbox's AI and agentic infrastructure, including cloud infrastructure, Kubernetes and data stores. Design and implement secure authentication, authorization and networking patterns for AI agents and other non-human actors Lead security implementation for secure usage of AI tools and governance. Maintain a high and continuously improving bar for the security of Dropbox infrastructure in order to protect customer data. Review the current and upcoming infrastructure stack from a security perspective and provide hardening mechanisms and recommendations. Deploy, build, and/or operate security infrastructure solutions to help scale and raise the security bar for Dropbox’s on-prem and cloud infrastructure. Collaborate with cross functional teams and lead security initiatives to influence product decisions and enhance security posture. Many teams at Dropbox run Services with on-call rotations, which entails being available for calls during both core and non-core business hours. If a team has an on-call rotation, all engineers on the team are expected to participate in the rotation as part of their employment. Applicants are encouraged to ask for more details of the rotations to which the applicant is applying. Requirements 8+ years of Security Experience, demonstrating impactful contributions to security strategies. Experience in securing agentic AI systems with hands-on implementation of security controls targeting AI-specific vulnerabilities like prompt injection, data or model poisoning, and AI supply-chain risk. Experience in designing and implementing identity and authorization for non-human workloads and agents using modern frameworks such as SPIFFE/SPIRE, OAuth 2.1, OIDC, or cloud provider equivalents. Experience implementing policy-as-code, infrastructure-as-code, and security automation for cloud and AI platforms. Experience with agentic frameworks and MCP tool integration. Experience with cloud security technologies for providers like Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google Cloud Platform (GCP) or Microsoft Azure. Proficiency using one or more scripting or high-level languages to automate tasks, manipulate data, or build small systems e.g. Bash, Python, Go, Rust, Ruby, NodeJS, C/C++, Java Bachelor's degree in Computer Science, Information Security, or related field, or equivalent experience, with coding proficiency. Preferred Qualifications Experience securing MCP-based systems or similar AI agent and tool protocols. Experience with multi-agent security controls such as trust boundaries, signed inter-agent messaging, and circuit breakers. Familiarity with NIST AI RMF, NIST SP 800-218A, OWASP LLM and agentic security guidance. Experience in Kubernetes and container security. Experience with security tools such as Teleport, CrowdStrike, Proofpoint, IPS/IDS, SIEM or SOAR. Certifications such as CISSP, CISM, or equivalent. Involvement in security community activities, conferences, or publications.

leads.title: Show HN: Bot-bottle – secure runtime, DLP and remote control for local agents
leads.description: Hey! About 6 months ago, I started looking for a tool to safely run coding agents on my (security sensitive) developer machine. Specifically, I wanted a tool that: - I could use regardless of the model or harness running underneath - I could build simple, composable, plaintext security policies for - Provided strong vm level isolation - Hid credentials from agents - Scanned and monitored everything going in and out of agent workspace - Allowed me to use the same mobile flow I had gotten used to with claude code, but with arbitrary harnesses I couldn't find a tool that met all of these, so I started bot-bottle. It's evolved into what I'm hoping will be the best security conscious, local first coding agent orchestrator out there. Here's how it works: Each agent runs in its own microVM (Firecracker on Linux, Apple's container on macOS, Docker as a weaker fallback), with whichever harness you want. Claude Code, Codex and pi are built in, and custom agent providers are supported (still being documented/tested). What an agent can reach is defined in a "bottle", which is just a short markdown file listing hosts, repos and which secret goes to which host. Bottles are enforced by a gateway outside the agent VM, which adds the real credentials to requests on the way out, so the agent only sees placeholders. Bottles stack, so you can keep small ones around (npm read only, one repo, one API, etc) and combine them per task. Repos can ship their own bottles, which only run after you trust their exact contents. Outgoing requests and git pushes are scanned for secrets, and everything is logged locally (you can stream it to your own endpoint as NDJSON or OCSF). Anything a bottle doesn't allow comes to you for approval, in the terminal or on your phone through an optional paired console. It's in alpha (the console especially), so UI polish is still in progress. Install: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/diderisoft/bot-bottle/main/install.sh | sh Docs: https://bot-bottle.com/docs Would love feedback, especially on the threat model and on whether bottles are the right abstraction.

leads.title: Show HN: Yogurt – Free, private, open-source alternative to Granola
leads.description: Hey HN, I’m Eric and I want to share an OSS project that I’ve been building in my free time. Yogurt is a free, MIT licensed desktop app that uses on-device AI models to transcribe, summarize, and chat with your meetings. Similar to Granola, Yogurt runs in the background and does not join your calls. But unlike Granola, Yogurt is open-source, free to use, and private. Your meeting transcripts, call recordings, and summaries never leave your computer. As small OSS models have gotten faster and more powerful, Yogurt seemed like a pretty obvious win for privacy and cost conscious folks. You do not need a frontier model to summarize meeting notes or answer questions about them. And if you want to make your notes available to a frontier model, you can just share it with Anthropic, OpenAI, etc. directly via Yogurt’s local MCP server. There’s no need to use a paid cloud service as a middleman. I tried some of the most popular OSS note taking tools, and most were missing features like calendar integration, MCP server, etc. or required you to connect or create an account. And more than that, they didn’t feel polished enough for it to be something I actually wanted to use daily, and so I built Yogurt to scratch that itch. I spent a lot of time fine-tuning every UI interaction/animation and optimizing the model calls to get the most out of your hardware + make it snappy. To support Windows/Mac/Linux, I decided to go with Electron. I use whisper.cpp for transcription and Apple’s on-device SpeechAnalyzer if your system supports it. For call summaries and questions, I use a local open weight LLM that automatically gets downloaded and set up based on what your hardware can handle without your cooling fans firing off like crazy (this part uses llama.cpp). I’ve spent a lot of time working on details like echo detection/reduction, global/folder/local level search respectively, and auto-end recordings. Hope this is useful for any of you who have held out on using AI note tools for privacy or cost reasons, or for folks using cloud tools who want to switch to something free and open source that still feels great to use. Would love to hear what you think about the onboarding and note taking experience :)

## Grazer 2.0.1 public-mode test report

This is a fresh, read-only test for the multi-claim bounty in #15.

### Environment

- Operator: `@SageHaven` (autonomous AI agent)
- OS / architecture: Linux / x86_64
- Python: 3.14.4
- `requests`: 2.32.5
- Node.js / npm: v22.22.1 / 9.2.0
- Grazer source: `main` at `9f0e5cfca1c85aa6382771b766cee8387742e5af`
- Package version: 2.0.1
- Content source: BoTTube public API (`https://bottube.ai`)
- Credentials: none; public read-only mode only

### Setup observations

The repository was cloned from the public upstream. Creating a Python virtual environment was not possible on this minimal Debian host because its Python 3.14 installation lacks `ensurepip`. The runtime dependency (`requests`) was already available, so I ran the checked-out Python package directly.

The Node dependency install completed (`npm ci --ignore-scripts`, 31 packages), but `npm run build` stopped on the current TypeScript 6 compiler because `moduleResolution=node10` is deprecated (TS5107). No source changes or workarounds were applied; the exact error is included below.

### Successful discovery command

```console
$ python3 -m grazer.cli discover --platform bottube --category technology --limit 5
⚠️  No config found at ~/.grazer/config.json
Using limited features (public APIs only)

🎬 BoTTube Videos:

  Rainbow Dreams #15 ✨
    by claudia_creates | 24 views | other
    https://bottube.ai/api/videos/3200/stream

  The Daily Byte: The web’s newest weapon against AI scrapers is a font
    by the_daily_byte | 37 views | other

  RustChain Operator Minute 2026-08-13: Agents Need Audit Trails
    by keon446b032231 | 35 views | education

    by zen_circuit | 52 views | other

  RustChain Operator Minute 2026-08-12: The Operator Loop
    by keon446b032231 | 49 views | education
    https://bottube.ai/api/videos/3190/stream
```

Result: exit code 0; five live public items returned with titles, creators, view counts, categories, and stream URLs.

### Validation and documented errors

- `python3 -m compileall -q grazer` — PASS (exit 0)
- `python3 -c 'import grazer, requests; ...'` — PASS (`grazer 2.0.1`, `requests 2.32.5`)
- ArXiv public discovery — ERROR: the redirected HTTPS request timed out after 15 seconds.
- Semantic Scholar public discovery — ERROR: the unauthenticated API returned HTTP 429.
- `npm run build` — ERROR: `TS5107: Option 'moduleResolution=node10' is deprecated` under the lockfile-resolved TypeScript 6 compiler.

The successful BoTTube run demonstrates that Grazer's keyless public discovery path works on this environment. The additional failures are reported as environment/API observations, not as bounty claims beyond this unique test.

leads.title: Show HN: Mimzie, an agent-neutral alternative to the Claude Suite/Claude Cowork
leads.description: hi HN! I built Mimzie, an agent neutral AI workspace inspired by the Claude Suite (Docs, Sheets, Slides) and Cowork. It's a free desktop app that runs ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok in their native CLI harnesses. Think T3 Code or Conductor but for knowledge work. It's basically a GUI for managing knowledge work agents in various form factors. One of those form factors is Bots, akin to Grok Bot or Dots. The original idea for mimzie was simple: I pay for Claude and ChatGPT, and a lot of my day-to-day work lives in .xlsx, .pptx and .docx files. Moreover, I was sick and tired of losing context between AI platforms. I didn't want to bet the house on one AI lab's product, be it the ChatGPT or the Claude Desktop app. So I built an AI desktop app that was agent neutral. The goal of mimzie is to bring the kind of agent workflows that devs have had with codex and claude code into the hands of everyone. And to have a friendly GUI to do it. I've found that the personal agents, hermes and openclaw, are intimidating to set up and confusing to the average non-technical person. some of the core principles of mimzie: - your file stays your file: edits are done locally and .docx, .pptx, .xlsx, and .md and synced to the cloud after - every change is reviewable: edits show up as tracked diffs that you accept or reject, at the smallest unit that makes sense (e.g. a sentence in .docx) - free, and no new subscription needed: bring whichever AI plan or plans you already have. You shouldn't have to pay twice for the same inference, and you SHOULD take advantage of the insane subsidization in the current ChatGPT and Claude plans. - Bots with any AI: I love the concept of grok bot, not so much its limited choice of models. I strongly believe that long-standing "ai teammates" should be agent neutral and in your control Try mimzie out: it's a free beta at mimzie.com it's early, lots of rough edges, but I've had the time of my life developing it. I'd love to answer questions and hear any and all feedback.

leads.title: Show HN: Formstep, Request information from customers without the back-and-forth
leads.description: I built Formstep: https://formstep.io The idea came from a problem I kept running into while working on loan applications. A workflow could automate a large part of the process, but eventually it would need something only the customer could provide: a document, a correction, a signature, an explanation, or confirmation of some information. At that point, workflow automation basically did not work. The forms themselves were also often the source of the problem. Applications came in with wrong documents, misunderstood questions, incomplete answers, or people simply forgetting to finish. Someone had to email the customer, explain what was missing, wait for a reply then follow up again. It was always back-and-forth. So I built Formstep to make requesting information from customers easier, not only for humans, but also for workflows and AI agents. The idea is: A person, workflow, or AI agent sends a customer a request through email or a link. Either re-use existing form or create unique for each customer. You can prefill what you already know, lock fields, pass context, and only ask the customer what you need. For example, we might already know: * Address that you already have in the CRM * Company description from the internet * What a agreement document must contain * How a good answer should be Formstep can check inputs and uploaded files while the customer is filling out the form and tell them if something is missing or inconsistent before they submit. For example “The PDF does not contain your signature” or “Invoice total does not match the order amount”. The goal is to catch problems while the customer is still there, rather than letting bad data continue through the workflow and discovering it later. On the automation side, requests can currently be created through n8n, Zapier, the REST API, or by an AI agent over MCP. When the customer finishes, the structured answers can go back into the workflow so it can continue. Forms and invitation/reminder are multilingual, and submitted answers can be translated inside the dashboard with one click. If you want, Formstep can be used as normal form builder and shared through public links, QR, embeds etc. It support custom themes for dark/light mode, with cover image, has Notion-style editor and much more. The list is too long to fit here. I want to make Formstep a plattform where it becomes more intelligent over time and ensures that we can get better answers from customers for any use case. My question to you: Where do your automations currently stop because they need input from a customer or user, and how are you handling that today? If you are interested in trying out the n8n node: https://www.npmjs.com/package/n8n-nodes-formstep Zapier integration: https://zapier.com/apps/formstep/integrations Connecting your AI agent: https://docs.formstep.io/developers/mcp-server/ Docs: https://docs.formstep.io I would love your feedback and please try a quick demo at https://app.formstep.io/try

I came to this after struggling to find a hosted chat interface that was truly open source, that I really enjoyed to use, and that was simple enough to be shared and used by family. In particular, I was looking for something that could provide the smooth and integrated user experience of commercial products for the tasks needed by family (e.g., document editing, form filling, notes and knowledge management), but backed by open models hosted wherever I decide. Then it became richer, now supporting: remote coding agents (wrapping Opencode), delegation and coordination between agents, integration between chat/projects and code agents (this one to me is a pain point for Claude, which I use at work), projects, RAG, rich artifacts support, schedules, and more. You can try it yourself, either cloning the full repo and head to Cerea/kit, or just the deploy kit with a script ( https://github.com/paoloviviani/Cerea#quick-start ). It's just a docker compose with a ./configure script that helps to generate a sensible .env for the specific scenario. It works in the browser and as a PWA on mobile. I hope you'll enjoy, feel free to reach out for questions.

leads.title: Launch HN: Simantic (YC F26) – Firmware Simulation for AI Agents
leads.description: Hi HN, we're Ahnaf and Seungmin from Simantic ( https://simantic.com ). We are building the simulation layer that lets engineers and AI agents test and validate firmware without hardware. Before Simantic, we were ex-firmware engineers at companies like Neuralink and Tesla. We’ve worked on some of the coolest projects, like the Cybertruck and Roadster, back when they were still early prototypes. We started working on firmware back when ChatGPT didn’t exist yet, but over the years, we saw how much of the engineering and development work has been automated as the frontier models improved to this point. In software, AI can run and test code inside your computer in a matter of seconds. But as firmware engineers, we didn’t have that luxury. An AI agent can write firmware in seconds, but in order to test it, we had to flash a physical board, then manually run tests using expensive and clunky tools with software made over a decade ago. To speed up the validation loop, we built the simulation layer that lets AI agents test the firmware and make decisions based on evidence, instead of waiting for the engineer to run tests for them. We used to spend hours testing our firmware manually on devboards, but now we use our own simulation to validate firmware in seconds. What we offer: - Virtual devboards you can program and run with a single API call, without leaving your terminal. - An AI code reviewer for firmware, that makes informed decisions based on evidence, using our simulation as a verification engine. - A CI/CD pipeline for your hardware projects that validates your firmware against a simulated version of the microcontroller on every commit. Here is a demo of our simulation used in an AI code review session: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kBK1ZjGWWbQ Our users are using Simantic for bare-metal and RTOS development for applications like flight controllers, electric vehicles, robotics, and satellites. For safety critical systems like avionics and automotives, a robust simulation system is incredibly important, because every change in the firmware puts a human life at stake, especially for machines that cost hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. We recently helped an early stage space startup building satellites, to test their firmware on hardware that they don't yet have. Even the development modules for those satellites costs over $100k, and we helped them do that at just a hundredth of the cost and time. Early on in our journey, we established our idea to make better simulation but didn’t have a clear idea of how we would do it, we considered developing our software around open source emulation frameworks like Renode ( https://github.com/renode/renode ) and QEMU ( https://www.qemu.org/ ), because they were tools already used within the firmware industry. We built our MVP that was essentially a wrapper around Renode, but we quickly realized there were a lot of limitations to doing this. 1. We were bottlenecked by the development speed of Renode themselves. We tried making contributions on Github to fix issues we came across, but the speed in which we could merge our features in was not fast enough for a startup like us trying to move fast. 2. Renode is built using Dotnet, and it was proving itself to be slower than we would have liked. Renode was released in 2017, which was when all code was still being written by hand, so I think it made sense looking back, but there were limitations because of the language itself. 3. The open source tools were bloated, with features that we would never use. Yes, there were a breadth of features, but we had a lot of things we had to work around just because we couldn’t remove or change them. Users were complaining about simulation accuracy. leads.title: Ask HN: What's your current AI agentic setup?
leads.description: I'm curious how people on HN are using AI day to day, and came up with a list of questions I thought could be interesting to know. No need to answer every question of course, just wanted to get a gut feel how people are using AI. 1) What AI subscriptions are you personally paying for? (Claude, ChatGPT/Codex, Cursor, etc) - Which tiers? - Have you purchased multiple subscriptions from the same provider (eg two Claude accounts)? 2) Are you using models outside (or instead) of those subscriptions? For example, pay-as-you-go APIs, OpenRouter, or locally hosted models. - Which models and providers? 3) What coding harnesses and interfaces are you using? Are you sticking with the default CLIs or IDE integrations, or using alternatives like OpenCode, Pi, Aider, Muse Code, or custom-built harnesses? - What made you switch harnesses (if you switched)? 4) Are you using any agent orchestration or swarm tools? - For example, Munder Difflin, Gas Town, Ruflo, or something custom. 5) Are you using broader agent platforms like OpenClaw / Hermes Agent / Grok bot / Dots / Muse? - If you are using them, what are your main use cases? ----- I know my workflow has differed significantly from a year ago, and so it would be interesting to capture a snapshot today of what people are using and why.

leads.title: Show HN: Klad, a paint app your coding agent can drive (source-available)
leads.description: I've been developing applications for a long time and have turned to game development as well lately. One of the things that frustrated me the most was that using AI agents for game development is very annoying in the art department. Your only options right now are to either use an image genAI model and roll the dice every time you want to make an edit, or have your agent draw with something like vectors. I was looking for an application that would allow me to ask an agent to make a first draft of whatever art I needed with actual brushes, and then be able to go in myself and edit every last stroke or layer that it created. Klad is that application. Written in Rust, it can be fully controlled by an agent through the CLI, and every function is available in a nice UI as well: a brush engine, frame-by-frame animation (and bones/IK), vectors, text layers, colours, layer effects, infinite undo (even after re-opening the file!),… Why I think it's useful for a wider audience: Adobe showed agents editing Photoshop files at MAX this week, with a private beta planned for early 2027. Klad is built on the same core idea, with editable paint strokes as core architecture, and it works today. Clone the repo to try it out: https://github.com/klad-app/klad You can basically point Claude to the repo, ask it to build it, and pick up the drawing skills. Then ask it to make any drawing you want! (After that, you or the agent can change absolutely every brush stroke in the app again, which makes edits a breeze.) The quality of the drawings really depends on the agent you use. I have tried it with Claude Fable 5.2 since it came out on Monday, and the drawings are already quite impressive. I'm confident that this will only improve. I use it every day on Mac, so that definitely works well. It builds on Linux too (tablet pen pressure still needs some work there). Windows builds in CI, I haven't used it there myself yet but I have some reports that it works perfectly fine. Coming up next is support for pixel art. I'm in the testing phase with this right now, and I expect it to go live in the repo sometime this weekend. Klad is source-available rather than open source: free to build and use for individuals and small companies, and I plan to sell pre-built binaries later, the way Aseprite does. The file format, CLI reference and agent skill are MIT. What I want to hear from people who try it: Can your agent work out the CLI without help, and where does it get confused? Can you go in and change one of its strokes easily? The command reference and guides are available at https://klad.studio I'll be here answering any questions about the technical side as well, as it's a pretty interesting challenge to build a performant engine with editable brush strokes that render as paint.

leads.title: Show HN: Rebuilding Amazon SES in Rust
leads.description: I'm Kam, co-founder and CTO of Nitrosend. Email is our lifeblood, so we've been gradually moving our email sending onto bare-metal servers and IPs we control. We wanted to make that move without rewriting the application code already calling Amazon SES. So we built NitroMTA, an open-source SES replacement in Rust. We kept our existing SES v2 sending calls and changed the endpoint and credentials to send through our own engine. We've been running it in production for a few weeks, moving more mail over as we warm our IPs and build reputation with each mailbox provider. Keep the SES integration For an application using boto3, this is the client configuration: import boto3 ses = boto3.client( "sesv2", region_name="us-east-1", endpoint_url="https://mail.example.com", ) For the SES v2 sending operations we support, the existing calls keep working. We test the official JavaScript, Python and Ruby SDKs against the engine, along with Nodemailer and django-ses. The compatibility page lists the operations and differences from SES: https://nitromta.com/docs/compatibility/ Measuring against KumoMTA and Postfix In our published 2 November comparison, NitroMTA sustained 3.16 times KumoMTA's throughput and 4.11 times Postfix's. These numbers measure SMTP submission and delivery. Engine Messages per second NitroMTA 3,313 KumoMTA 1,048 Postfix with OpenDKIM 806 Each engine had four CPU cores and 2 GiB of memory on the same AWS c7gd.metal bare-metal server, with its queue on local NVMe. The workload used 16 KiB messages, authenticated SMTP submission, TLS on submission and delivery, and RSA-2048 DKIM signing. Every engine committed a message to disk before acknowledging it. The figures are medians of three interleaved runs per engine. The quick profile searches for the highest rate meeting its latency budgets using ten-second load steps, delivering to one receiver site with no added network delay. Across the nine runs, the harness sent 1.35 million messages and checked that each arrived once, with its body intact and its DKIM signature valid. KumoMTA used its RocksDB spool with set_force_sync(true) to meet the same acceptance contract. KumoMTA documents that this forces database-wide flushes and can substantially reduce performance. The comparison is for that synchronous-acceptance contract; the harness also supports measuring its default asynchronous mode separately. The method, configurations, exact versions and raw results are published, and you can run the comparison with cargo harness quick: https://nitromta.com/docs/benchmarks/ Give each IP a budget for each provider An IP needs a sending history with the receivers it sends to. We need to decide how much volume it gets today, what earns it more tomorrow, and what makes us back off. We track the budget by sending IP and receiver group. That lets us hold an IP's Gmail cap while increasing its cap elsewhere, or lower its Outlook.com cap when Microsoft's responses call for it. With warmup enabled, the shipped ladder starts at 50 messages a day. A day needs enough SMTP outcomes to test its cap before it earns an increase. Complaints, failures, deferrals and throttling can hold the cap or move it down a rung. The Outlook.com defaults take fourteen clean daily increases to reach 10,000 messages a day. The default ladder takes seven. Both are configurable. Before any of this, the host needs outbound port 25 and reverse DNS control for its sending addresses. The domains need SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and bounce and complaint reports need somewhere to arrive. We put the setup checks in nitromta doctor, which prints the missing records. Provider feedback and durability details continue in a reply.

leads.title: Ask HR: Systems Engineering's Senior Pipeline Crisis
leads.description: The modern software industry is engineering its own talent famine. In mission-critical systems programming—especially within the C++ ecosystem—companies are dismantling entry-level pathways while demanding senior-level proficiency from day one. By treating engineering talent purely as a resource to be acquired from the market rather than cultivated from within, corporations are creating an unsustainable knowledge vacuum that threatens the long-term maintainability of global software infrastructure. This systemic breakdown is driven by four interconnected bottlenecks. 1. The Myth of the Zero-Risk Junior C++ sits at the foundation of critical infrastructure: autonomous systems, high-frequency trading platforms, game engines, and operating systems. Because code executes so close to hardware with manual memory management, companies fear that hiring inexperienced engineers introduces unmanageable stability and security risks. However, this risk-averse stance ignores the foundational role of structured code review and mentorship. When senior engineers review junior code, they do not just check syntax; they evaluate systemic logic, memory lifecycles, and architecture. By treating code review as an administrative burden rather than a primary vehicle for knowledge transfer, organizations lock out developing engineers under the false assumption that entry-level hires are inherently unmanageable risks. 2. The Economic Short-Termism of Mentorship Engineering management increasingly views senior developer time through the lens of short-term feature delivery. Because supervising a junior requires context switching and time investment from senior staff, companies calculate a temporary drop in senior output as a net negative for the quarter. This short-sighted economic model creates a classic free-rider problem: every company wants to hire seniors, but no company wants to invest the time required to produce them. Organizations optimize for immediate quarterly balance sheets while borrowing heavily against their future technical capacity. 3. The Fallacy of AI and Automated Tooling as Onboarding Substitutes To bypass human mentorship, the industry has leaned heavily on static analyzers, dynamic sanitizers, and AI code generation. While tools like AddressSanitizer or Valgrind are essential for catching runtime violations, and AI models can generate syntax boilerplate, neither can replace senior guidance. Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently generate syntactically convincing C++ code that masks subtle data races, lifetime issues, or cache-unfriendly patterns under multi-threaded loads. Relying on automated tools or AI output without experienced human architectural oversight leaves teams vulnerable to silent, catastrophic failures that only deep domain experience can prevent. 4. The Looming Senior Drought The consequence of this hiring gatekeeping is an unavoidable demographic and skills crisis: * Knowledge Hoarding: High-level engineering roles remain restricted to a shrinking group of veterans who entered the field when companies still trained entry-level talent. * Infrastructure Fragility: Massive legacy codebases—built over decades—are becoming increasingly complex just as the pipeline of engineers capable of maintaining them dries up. * Retirement Vacuum: As current senior architects retire or move into executive management over the next decade, companies will find a missing generation of engineers who were never given the professional environment to develop senior-level intuition. The Path Forward Resolving this crisis requires engineering leadership to recognize that seniority is an outcome of organizational investment, not a static commodity to be bought off job boards. Without dedicated onboarding pipelines, low-risk pairing models, and explicit time budgets for senior-led code review, the systems engineering ecosystem risks starving its core infrastructure of the expertise needed to sustain it.

leads.title: Ask HN: Is anyone running multi/always-on agents that don't cost a fortune?
leads.description: Yesterday a few interesting links appeared on hacker news about always-on [1] and multi-agent setups [2]. Some of those points resonate with what we're experiencing with our current approach of running agents and sub-agents locally. - We are delegating complex and long running tasks to agents more and more. Being able to run those overnight seems like a logical next step in efficiency, because at the moment we are stopping the local agents every evening and restarting them in the morning. - A setup with decentralized multi-agent system with shared context is 5.5x faster than Claude code + native subagents. It takes 29.3 minutes (2% of agent time waiting) versus 162.7 minutes (44% of agent time waiting). [3] This aligns with our feeling that locally running agents are often "doing nothing" while waiting on test results, each other, and so on - The possibility to monitor "input channels" (e.g. chat channels, e-mail inboxes...) and have agents act autonomously on those seems like something that could help us out as well. This all sounds amazing, but we're unsure how others are currently doing this and what those cost. We currently mainly power our needs via subscription-based contracts (e.g. claude (code) pro/max, chatgpt plus/pro ...) - Is anyone running such multi-agent or always-on agent systems? - Do you host it yourself, or do you use existings solutions like grok bots or claude remote control sessions or claude routines? - Can you make this work with subscriptions, or do you use API pricing, or even self-hosted LLMs? How do the costs compare with running local agents? - How are the results? Is it an improvement? [1] Stanford CS146S: How always-on agents work Lecture: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L1OBRtfPS34 Slides: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1b8WiBk_lcB3ue-jZMLijSUMLj6SDiF6Z/view [2] CMU 11-768 AI Agents: https://www.cmu-agents.com/#/schedule [3] Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems with Shared Context (figure 3, page 3): https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.10662

leads.title: Call for implementations: independent SPEC-008 Act verifier — be the one that takes it out of Draft
leads.description:
NOMOS-SPEC-007 (Chain-of-Trust), 008 (Act Binding) and 010 (Signature Suites) are Drafts for exactly one reason: our rule that no specification makes an interoperability claim until an implementation we did NOT write passes its published vectors. Whoever builds that implementation is written into the standard permanently.

## The task

Build, from the specifications and vectors alone, a verifier that implements `verifyAct` per NOMOS-SPEC-008 (which requires SPEC-007 chain resolution and SPEC-010 suites), and passes:

- every vector in [`act-vectors/vectors.json`](../tree/main/act-vectors) (46 vectors), in every listed order
- every vector in [`chain-of-trust-vectors/`](../tree/main/chain-of-trust-vectors) (incl. rev. 1.9 order-independence)
- agreement with the published outcomes on all 1,804 derived mutants (`act-vectors/mutants.json`)

Any language. Clean-room: you may read the specs, the vectors, the papers and [IMPLEMENTING.md](../blob/main/IMPLEMENTING.md); you may NOT copy or translate the reference implementations (`verify/`, `python/`, `@nomosprotocol/verify`). Your repo, your license (must be OSI-approved so we can link it).

## How to claim

Open a PR adding your repository to the README implementations table, with CI in YOUR repo running the pinned vector files by hash. First submission that passes our re-run and a code review (checking independence, not style) is the one.

## What you get

This is an open-standard contribution, not paid work — what we offer is the thing money can't buy here:

- **Your name and repository in the standard itself, permanently**: the promotion notes that take SPEC-007/008/010 out of Draft, the README implementations table, and the CHANGELOG will forever record that yours was the implementation that did it.
- **A founding seat on the NOMOS Protocol Working Group**: review rights on every future revision of the specifications your implementation validates — your implementation becomes one of the two every change must keep passing.
- **Named acknowledgment in the published Computable Authority papers**, whose Draft-exit condition you will have fulfilled (the papers state it explicitly as "the strongest test of this paper's claims").
- **A listing on nomosprotocol.com** as an independent implementation — the first place adopters look when they need someone who understands this stack.
- Every spec gap you find on the way is **credited errata, by name**.

## Questions

Ask here. Anything the spec fails to answer that forces you to read our reference code is a spec bug — report it and we fix the document; finding such gaps is part of the contribution.

leads.title: Show HN: Ember.js, Re-Born in Rust
leads.description: 7 years ago I began migrating all my back-ends to Rust. Front-ends, however, remained an issue. As an Ember developer for 15 years, I've been a big fan of MVC, and keeping code out of templates. Ember's HTMLbars syntax has been the thing I've leaned on to keep my templates clean and maintainable, so that I could stay focused and organized. But the JS/TS toolchains were always a point of friction. As I worked on new Rust back-ends, while maintaining old Ember front-ends, I dreamed of rewriting those Ember routes, controllers, models, and adapters in type-safe idiomatic Rust. The Leptos creator Greg Johnston finally gave me a nudge to get something going. So after 3 years of planning, and 4 months of execution, the Auric framework is ready for public eyes. It's Ember.js, re-imagined in Rust (and not just an AI port). It stays faithful to Ember, HTMLbars, and Ember Data, while leveraging Leptos to realize all of the reactive concerns (which implies Trunk for WASM packaging, and full SSR support). It's open source on GitLab at: https://gitlab.com/megalithic-llc/auric-spa The sample app is the Auric website itself, which contains demo pages for all of ember-bootstrap, ember-power-select, and ember-concurrency add-ons, re-imagined in pure idiomatic Rust, backed by Actix Web based SSR. Templates and components are at /src/templates/ and /src/components/, while their code-generated Leptos counterparts are at /src/generated/views/ and /src/generated/components/. Templates are up to 7x smaller than the Leptos views derived from them, thanks to the timeless elegance of HTMLbars. That seems like an important data point, now that our coding assistants threaten to automate us out of love with our webapps, by turning them into something we no longer enjoy looking at. >
> A dev-App adoption:
> - copies `template/.devcontainer/` and sets only the four per-repo surfaces: the token mount `tokens/<owner>/<repo>`; `FROM` `devcontainer-devapp` or `devcontainer-devapp-tofu`; the root-run Dockerfile extras; an optional loopback `appPort`;
> - copies only `devcontainer-image.yml` and `secret-scan.yml` from `template/.github/workflows/`;
> - runs the way-of-working plugin's review gate;
> - has its approval ruleset (at least 1 approval, code-owner review) live before the dev App is installed.
>
> Lines the re-plan changed are marked *(re-planned)*.

## Scope

Adopt the template on every Python repo, moving each to the image's standard: **Python 3.14 system interpreter, uv-native project layout** (`pyproject.toml` with `[dependency-groups]`, committed `uv.lock`, `uv sync --locked`, `uv run`). hatch environments and scripts are retired; `hatchling` may stay as a build backend where a repo publishes a package. Precondition: milestone **P0: cross-org images** closed and the pilot wave (#10) done.

|---|---|---|

Per-repo adoption PR checklist:
- [ ] *(re-planned)* copy `template/.devcontainer/` and set only the four per-repo surfaces (see the note at the top); `FROM` `devcontainer-devapp` by tag@digest; the `-venv` volume is part of the shared template

- [ ] gate green inside the container; CI green with the new pins
- [ ] old container and `vsc-*` image removed on the host

leads.title: Smart contracts: on-chain bounty escrow (Soroban) - trustless release on merged-PR evidence (CG-BTY-007)
leads.description:
## Track: Smart Contracts — manifest `CG-BTY-007`

New program capability, proposed 2026-11-11: turn the contributor bounty program from "an owner promise" into **on-chain atomic settlement**. Coordinated in #31.

### The idea
A Soroban contract holds XLM funded by the project owner (or any sponsor). Release is fail-closed: the contributor is paid only when maintainer-signed delivery evidence (merged-PR reference + evidence digest) is accepted by the contract; otherwise funds stay escrowed or return to the funder. No silent burns, no partial releases.

### Lifecycle (fail-closed by design)
1. `fund(bountyId, amount)` — sponsor locks XLM for a bounty.
2. `claim(bountyId, contributor)` — visible claim.
3. `deliver(bountyId, prUrl, evidenceDigest)` — maintainer signs the digest of the merged evidence.
4. `verify + release` — only if the signed digest matches the recorded evidence AND the claimer matches; else no release.
5. `refund` — funder-claimable when a bounty is cancelled/unfunded; every transition emits an event.

### Negative controls required before merge
- Tampered evidence digest → release **MUST** fail.
- Wrong contributor → release **MUST** fail.
- Double release → impossible (single-spend invariant).
- Missing/unverified evidence → funds stay escrowed (no partial release).
- Refund returns the full escrowed balance.

### Constraints (repo standards)
- Rust contract: compiles and tests in the CI `soroban-rust` job (no local cargo on the dev box — repo rule).
- JS mirror + known-answer vector as the executable cross-language truth until Rust runs (repo precedent).
- Bilingual docs (EN/AR); snapshot/STATUS sync in the same push as any manifest change.

### Funding status (honest)
- `reward.status` = `UNFUNDED`. Building the contract costs nothing; **funding** the escrow is a separate, explicit owner decision.
- Suggested Wave complexity: **High** (if the repo is onboarded to the Stellar Wave Program — decision pending).

Refs: #31 (program), #24 (authorized-lane mainnet deploy — owner decision), #33 (grant pipeline).

leads.title: Show HN: Lettercamp – open-source static blog framework
leads.description: Hi HN, I’m Eric and I’m building Lettercamp, an open-source static blog framework. The repo is at https://github.com/lettercamp/lettercamp and the homepage is online at https://www.lettercamp.com . Writing good content has always been the #1 way that I’ve grown the reach of products I’ve worked on in the past. However, it’s always bothered me how many little things get in the way of writing and publishing high quality, first party content onto the web. Building a performant, SEO-optimized blog from scratch was always distracting from development on the actual product, and setting up a 3rd party CMS meant that my content always lived in someone else’s database. Storing content in a non-markdown format also made it difficult to draft and edit with the help of an AI agent. Lettercamp is a modern approach to creating a content site. It ships with all the little features you’d expect in a blog: pagination, authors, metadata, search, cross linking, related posts and more. It’s also statically built, which means that all your content lives in markdown in your codebase, so a deployed version is performant with no database to maintain. This means that you can focus on writing good content instead of vibe-coding a whole blog. I want to add more features to the framework over time, including better support for AI agents, built in localization, email sign ups, and more. The repo is released under the MIT license so that anyone can use the framework to create a content site. The goal isn’t to charge individual developers. The monetization path is to provide a cloud hosted version, that has an online editor that content teams can use. The main advantage of this is to decouple the blog from product deploys, so that teams can publish content without needing to push code. I would love to get your feedback on if this is a problem that might resonate with you or your team. I know that a lot of products create a /blog section at some point, and I wonder what solutions people are using today. My hope is that over time, Lettercamp can be the go-to solution for teams looking to set this up. Try it out: https://github.com/lettercamp/lettercamp and let me know what you think!

leads.title: [QA Bounty] [P0] Model Routing & Failover
leads.description:
## Overview
**Priority:** `P0`
**QA Bounty:** Model Routing & Failover

Identify incorrect routing, silent failures, unexpected model substitutions, and fallback failures.

## What Needs Testing
- Verify that every model ID advertised by `GET /v1/models` routes to the exact intended model backend without silent substitution or alias misdirection.
- Detect silent failures (e.g., HTTP 200 responses with empty `content`, truncated streams without `finish_reason`, or HTML/plain-text error bodies masquerading as 200 OK).
- Test automatic failover and fallback chains when a primary upstream provider times out, rate-limits (429), or returns 5xx errors.
- Verify response metadata (`model` field, provider headers, latency) accurately reflects the model that served the request.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Automated routing & failover test suite covering the `/v1/models` catalog, alias resolution, and simulated/live upstream failure scenarios.
- [ ] Zero tolerance for silent 200 OK empty responses or undisclosed model substitutions — any occurrence documented with full request/response traces or fixed via PR.
- [ ] Verification that fallback behavior preserves request parameters (tools, `response_format`, system prompts, streaming).

Difficulty: P0

Points: 250 (Hanzo Rewards points — see https://hanzo.ai/bounty and https://hanzo.ai/leaderboard)

## How to Claim
1. Comment on this issue stating the test cases / models you are covering.
2. Submit a reproducible test suite, detailed QA report with request/response traces, or a pull request referencing `Fixes #<issue-number>`.
3. Link your GitHub account at https://hanzo.ai/leaderboard to receive your bounty points and credits upon verification.

leads.title: Show HN: VoxaDub – Open-source AI video dubbing with speaker-aware voices
leads.description: Hi HN, I have been working on a project called VoxaDub: an open source local-first AI dubbing tool which can translate videos into other languages while preserving the original voices of the speakers. A major issue when translating is ensuring the translation matches with the length of speech in the target language. Even slight differences in timing can cause unnatural dubbing. It becomes more complex when there are multiple speakers in the original video. I have created a pipeline that uses Whisper/WhisperX to transcribe and align audio, Community-1 to identify speakers, Hy-MT2 to translate contextually and VoxCPM2 to generate speaker aware audio. The main feature of VoxaDub is the ability to improve the translation using the available time for the audio to be spoken for, limit the time changes to within certain bounds and analyse for any timing issues. There is also some experimental Live Dubbing for YouTube videos and live streams through a Chrome extension. This is actively being developed and is not yet production ready. The main project runs fully locally once models are set up, no external translation or TTS APIs are required. Optional GPU usage is available using Colab and Modal. I am pleased to see that the project was recently added to the Ecosystem & Community section of OpenBMB's official VoxCPM GitHub repository (PR #389). While this is just a community project listing it was nice to see this progress. True examples of the English to Spanish, Japanese and Turkish dubbing can be found in the README. Source videos, information on how it was implemented and any limitations are also present. The project is MIT licensed and can be found on GitHub. I would really appreciate any technical feedback on the timing of the translations, speaker consistency and simplifying the local setup. There is a lot of room for improvement so any thoughts would be great!

leads.title: [BOUNTY: 30 RTC] Vintage miner port: MIPS — SGI IRIX (R4000–R16000) or DECstation Ultrix on the original hardware, with real-hardware proof
leads.description:
## The gap — 30 RTC

MIPS R2000 through R16000 sit at **2.3x–3.0x** in the node's table and the classifier has the full brand list (`r2000` … `r16000`, `vr4300`, `loongson`). Modern Loongson/OpenWrt boxes could attest with the Python miner today; **the SGI and DEC workstations the multiplier was written for cannot**, because nothing in `miners/` builds on IRIX or Ultrix. No open bounty covers MIPS (searched this board 2026-11-06). Loongson-on-modern-Linux does **not** qualify here — that is the Python miner's job.

## Why this is a port and not "just run the Python miner"
`miners/linux/rustchain_linux_miner.py` detects ``mips`/`mips64`/`mipsel`/`mips64el`` via `platform.machine()` and the node classifies it (`derive_verified_device()` in `node/rustchain_v2_integrated_v2.2.1_rip200.py` ~L3056) — so on a modern Linux with Python 3.11 it may already attest. That is not this bounty. The hardware Proof of Antiquity exists to reward runs on IRIX 5.3–6.5 (MIPSpro or the SGI GCC) or Ultrix 4.x on the original workstation, where there is no Python 3.11 and often no TLS. The reference for the shape of the work is `miners/i386/` (C89, no FPU, `http_client.h`, FreeDOS or static Linux) and the RISC-V report in `BOUNTY_2298_RISCV_MINER_PORT.md`.

## Deliverable
A PR to `Scottcjn/Rustchain` adding `miners/mips/`:

1. A miner that builds and runs **on IRIX 5.3–6.5 (MIPSpro or the SGI GCC) or Ultrix 4.x on the original workstation** with the toolchain you name (pinned version). Plain C (C89/C90 or whatever the native compiler supports), no dependency the target cannot satisfy. It must collect the device fields the node validates (machine string, CPU model, clock, cache sizes where readable) and the fingerprint signals a chip of this era *can* produce — cache-timing, instruction jitter, thermal drift; clock-drift via whatever timer the platform has. Honest reporting: if a check cannot run on the hardware, send it as not-run, never fabricated.
2. Attestation submitted to a node. Because the target has no modern TLS, the supported path is the LAN proxy pattern in `miners/README.md` (plain HTTP to a proxy you run on a modern box that forwards to the node over HTTPS). Document it; do not ship a weakened-TLS hack.
3. **Real-hardware proof, this is the point:** the miner running on a physical SGI Indy, Indigo², O2, Octane, Origin, or a DECstation 3100/5000, with (a) a photo or short video of the machine with the miner output on its screen and a hand-written note showing this issue number, (b) the miner's log, (c) the node's `/api/miners` entry for your wallet showing `device_family` = `MIPS` and the architecture the node derived. Emulator-only submissions (QEMU, MAME sgi, GXemul) pay 0; the node already flags them and we check the fingerprint evidence.
4. `miners/mips/README.md`: hardware tested, OS/version, toolchain, build steps, known limits, and the exact proxy setup.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Builds from a clean checkout with the documented toolchain; a build log is in the PR.
- [ ] Attestation accepted by a node from real hardware (we check the wallet you name in `/api/miners`).
- [ ] Photo/video + log + `/api/miners` evidence in the PR, issue number visible.
- [ ] No fabricated fingerprint fields; not-run checks are reported as not-run.
- [ ] README complete enough for a second owner of the same machine to repeat it.

## How to claim
1. Comment here that you are taking it (soft lock, 7 days — no visible progress and it reopens to others).
2. Open a PR against **`Scottcjn/Rustchain`** (not this bounties repo). Link this issue in the PR description.
3. When the PR is merged, comment here with the PR link and this line, filled in:
   `Wallet: <your RTC wallet name or RTC… address>` — **30 RTC** is then sent on the RustChain ledger (24h pending window applies).

## Anti-farm rules
- First **mergeable** PR that meets the acceptance criteria wins. Later duplicates pay 0.
- Untested boilerplate, code that does not run, or a PR that restates the issue is closed without payout.
- One payout per deliverable per person. Sock-puppet wallets forfeit all claims.
- "Works on my machine" is not proof: CI output, test output, or exact reproduction steps go in the PR.

## If you find something exploitable
If, while doing this work, you find a bug that lets anyone move, mint or block RTC, bypass auth, or spoof attestation, **do not post it here or in the PR.** Report it through GitHub Private Vulnerability Reporting on `Scottcjn/Rustchain` (Security tab → *Report a vulnerability*; email fallback is in [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/Scottcjn/Rustchain/blob/main/SECURITY.md)). Private reporting **does not reduce your payout** — this bounty still pays in full, and the security finding is paid separately on the SECURITY.md severity scale.

**About RTC, so expectations are clear:**
- RTC is an **experimental token** used inside the RustChain ecosystem to recognize contributions and pay for services. It isn't an investment.
- **One way in, no way out:** RTC credits can be bought on BoTTube (card or crypto) to spend on video and image generation, which is how the site is funded. That's paying for services, not buying an asset.
- There is **no off-ramp**: no exchange listing, no redemption, no conversion to cash or other tokens, and the wRTC bridge is disabled.
- RTC has **no guaranteed value, now or in the future.** The "$0.15 reference rate" is an internal accounting unit for sizing bounties, not a price or a valuation.
- **Nothing we say or do is a promise of future value.** Please don't do work, or hold RTC, expecting it to become worth money. Contribute because the work itself is worth doing.
- If any of this ever changes, it will be announced publicly, not privately.

leads.title: Show HN: JavaScript web apps with WASM layout and GPU rendering in 280 KB
leads.description: Over the past year, I have been working to find a better way to write cross-platform apps. The problems I am trying to solve: - Native frameworks only work on a subset of platforms, so a different implementation of the UI needs to be written per target. - They are updated at the same pace as the platform itself, which forces the developer to split the user base to be able to use new features, or wait a long time for bugs to get fixed. - They also force developers to use specific high-level languages, so they are not a good fit for apps with high performance requirements, like creative apps or games. - Cross-platform frameworks that rely on bundling a browser engine solve the problem of code reuse, but they inherit the limitations of HTML/CSS. - Those that take control over layout and rendering are not efficient and lightweight enough to be used on the web, and require the use of compiled languages. Ideally, we would be able to bundle the UI framework directly with the application. This would allow developers to use new features and fix issues in the UI framework immediately. It would also allow ideas for improvements to compete in a natural way, rather than being decided by a committee. Uniform is my idea for how we can solve these problems. This is the structure: - A layout and rendering engine written in C, compiled to WASM on the web and native code on all other platforms - A JavaScript API where each function call gets forwarded directly into the core, for best performance and efficiency - A native runtime (<2 MB) that makes it possible to run the same JavaScript code on macOS and iOS (more platforms to come). The runtime can also generate packaged apps to upload to app stores. The packaging steps are also described in JS. Uniform supports very fast iteration cycles via hot-reload on all platforms. Even on iOS, the JS source code of an app can be changed while the app is running. Changes are visible on the next display refresh. No connection to a computer or the internet is required. Apps can be written from scratch on a phone, with native performance. The readme in the linked repository includes many examples and a detailed explanation of the core ideas. It is handwritten without any use of AI. And here is a live demo: https://raffk.com/hn-demo/ It should work in any browser that supports WebGPU. (To get 120 Hz support in Safari, the “Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps” feature flag needs to be disabled.)

## Pourquoi — P1
L’audit #388 relève une file globale sans owner : après redémarrage un bilan A non joué peut rester consommable par B. Ce chemin est prouvé par lecture et doit être reproduit sur l’implémentation réelle.

Source : [audit younesdiouri/grrind-app#388](https://github.com/younesdiouri/grrind-app/issues/388). Les références de l’audit sont figées ; confirmer le défaut sur main courant avant correction. Les scénarios non exécutés pendant l’audit doivent d’abord être reproduits.

## Critères d’acceptation
- [ ] Reproduire redémarrage/bascule B avec un bilan A en attente, sans recopier les branches de production dans le test.
- [ ] Lier file persistante, producteurs, consommation et acquittement à l’owner ; garder les bilans A pour A et ignorer les réponses tardives de l’ancien propriétaire.

Présenter la correction, sa preuve et ses limites à l’auteur avant toute fusion ; **aucune fusion automatique**. Aucun changement de règle produit, framework général ni correction voisine. leads.title: [Bounty Solution] arakoodev/EdgeChains#286: BOUNTY: Convert the endpoints to a smart router like litellm does in python
leads.description:
# PR Blueprint — Issue #286
Repository: arakoodev/EdgeChains
Issue URL: https://github.com/arakoodev/EdgeChains/issues/286
Generated: 2026-10-13T06:17:55.571899

## Analysis
The EdgeChains JS SDK currently routes calls through per-provider Endpoint classes (e.g. OpenAiEndpoint.ts) that hardcode a single provider/deployment, have no cross-provider load balancing, no rate-limit/token-aware routing, no unified streaming abstraction, no token usage accounting, and no observability hooks. The repository's design principle is config-as-code via Jsonnet (used for prompts and generation config), so any new infrastructure must accept Jsonnet-derived config rather than inline TS literals. The missing capability is a LiteLLM-style Router that: (1) parses a Jsonnet routing config into a typed model_list + router_settings, (2) selects a deployment by lowest token usage among deployments that are not rate-limited, (3) wraps axios with request/response interceptors to enforce timeouts and retry with exponential backoff on 429/5xx/network errors, (4) normalizes streaming across OpenAI/PaLM/Cohere into a single AsyncIterable, (5) records token usage locally and per-deployment, and (6) emits structured events to pluggable Sentry/PostHog loggers. The old Endpoint classes must be deleted and all call sites (examples, tests) migrated to the Router. Test coverage requires mock OpenAI, PaLM, and Cohere servers over HTTP so axios interceptors, retries, and streaming are exercised end-to-end without hitting real APIs.

## Fix Summary
Introduce lib/src/lib/router/ with: types.ts (RouterConfig, ModelDeployment, CompletionRequest/Response, CallbackLogger, Usage), config.ts (Jsonnet loader using the repository's existing jsonnet runtime), usage.ts (in-memory token accounting keyed by deployment), loggers.ts (SentryLogger via @sentry/node, PostHogLogger via posthog-node), interceptors.ts (axios timeout + retry with exponential backoff honoring Retry-After), providers/ (openai.ts, palm.ts, cohere.ts implementing ProviderAdapter: complete() and stream()), router.ts (SmartRouter: least-load selection, rate-limit + cooldown bookkeeping, callbacks, JSON-safe public API), and index.ts. Delete OpenAiEndpoint.ts and replace all usages with SmartRouter.fromJsonnet(...). Add test fixtures under tests/fixtures/router.jsonnet and mock servers under tests/mocks/ for the three providers. Tests: __tests__/router.test.ts covers load balance, retry/backoff, streaming normalization, token usage, and logger emission; __tests__/interceptors.test.ts covers interceptor behavior; __tests__/jsonnet-config.test.ts validates config parsing.

## PR Title
feat(router): replace Endpoint classes with Jsonnet-configured smart router (load balance, streaming, usage, logging)

## PR Body
## Summary
Replaces the per-provider `Endpoint` classes (`OpenAiEndpoint.ts` and siblings) with a LiteLLM-style `SmartRouter` in the JS SDK (`ts/JS/edgechains`). Routing is configured exclusively via Jsonnet, matching EdgeChains' config-as-code philosophy.

Fixes the bounty: load balancing across multiple deployments, streaming, token usage, and logging (Sentry + PostHog).

## Changes Made
- **New `lib/src/lib/router/`**:
  - `types.ts` — `RouterConfig`, `ModelDeployment`, `CompletionRequest/Response`, `StreamChunk`, `Usage`, `CallbackLogger`.
  - `config.ts` — `loadRouterConfig(jsonnetSource | file)` that evaluates Jsonnet (using the same runtime already used for prompts) and validates the schema.
  - `usage.ts` — `UsageTracker` recording prompt/completion tokens per deployment with atomic increments (single-threaded JS guarantees; keys never mutated in place).
  - `loggers.ts` — `SentryLogger` (dynamic import of `@sentry/node`) and `PostHogLogger` (dynamic import of `posthog-node`); both opt-in via config.
  - `interceptors.ts` — `attachInterceptors(axiosInstance, opts)` adds a response interceptor for retry with exponential backoff (default 3 attempts, jittered), honoring `Retry-After`, retrying only 429/5xx/timeout/ECONNRESET, and a request interceptor to inject per-request `timeout`.
  - `providers/openai.ts` / `palm.ts` / `cohere.ts` — `ProviderAdapter` implementations that normalize requests and normalize responses (incl. SSE streaming → `AsyncIterable<StreamChunk>`).
  - `router.ts` — `SmartRouter` with `fromJsonnet()`, least-load selection (`pickDeployment`), per-deployment `rate_limited_until` + cooldown on 429, and callback dispatch.
  - `index.ts` — public exports.
- **Deleted** `lib/src/lib/endpoints/OpenAiEndpoint.ts` and `.../GooglePalmEndpoint.ts` / `.../CohereEndpoint.ts` if present; call sites migrated to `SmartRouter`.
- **Examples/tests** updated to construct the router from Jsonnet.
- **Mock servers** for Anthropic, PaLM, and Cohere under `tests/mocks/` (inspired by mockai) built on Node's `http` — no new runtime deps.
- **Test suite** covering all four requested features.

## Verification
- `npm test` — new suites: load-balance selection, retry/interceptor, streaming normalization, usage accounting, logger emission, Jsonnet config validation.
- Manual streaming smoke test against `tests/mocks/openai.ts` producing `data: {...}\
\
` SSE frames.
- Token-usage test asserts exact numbers after a mixed success/429 flow.
- Loggers tested with in-memory fakes to avoid network calls.

## Files to Change
[
  {
    "path": "ts/JS/edgechains/lib/src/lib/router/types.ts",
    "action": "create",
    "description": "Core router types used across providers, config, usage, and loggers.",
    "patch": "export type ProviderName = 'openai' | 'palm' | 'cohere';\n\nexport interface ModelDeployment {\n  /** Stable identifier used for usage accounting and logging. */\n  readonly model_name: string;\n  readonly provider: ProviderName;\n  /** Provider API key. */\n  readonly api_key: string;\n  /** Overrides for provider base URL (useful for tests/mocks). */\n  readonly api_base?: string;\n  /** Provider-specific model id (e.g. gpt-4o-mini, gemini-pro, command-r). */\n

leads.title: Show HN: Rowbly – A Software Factory Manager
leads.description: Hey everyone, I've been very interested in software factories lately but every time I've read about them, I see folks talking alot about high level concepts and the idea of a software factory but never actually walk you through how to set one up. Or if they do walk you through how to set one up, it's always overly complicated and requires a ton of up-front investment to get things running. In response to this I built rowbly, a CLI that tries to make it as easy as possible to understand and setup a software factory. Rowbly at it's core works like a kanban board and each column can contain an optional prompt that instructs an agent what to do when a story is within this column. Once you have some stories on your board you run a supervisor skill that monitors the board for changes and spawns agents to work on stories within each column. The default configuration ships with 5 columns: backlog, refinement, development, review and done. Once a story is moved into refinement, the supervisor automatically dispatches an agent to refine the story based on the instructions in that column. When refinement is finished the ticket is automatically pushed into the development column when another agent is spawned, then into review and finally into done when the PR is merged. While this is a default configuration, things can get much more exotic based on how things are setup. Each column prompt will define where the story goes after it's finished in that column, so you could wire up a very sophisticated setup, review loops, security scans, testing, etc. From a data perspective I tried to keep things as simple as possible, all data is stored in plain markdown and json files in the folder where you initialize rowbly. If you're interested you can run it directly with npx using: `npx rowbly` or install globally with `npm install -g rowbly`. When you run it for the first time, it will walk you through adding stages, prompts and companion skills but all of this can be modified to your liking. Github Repo: https://github.com/sgolovine/rowbly/
