leads.title: Anthropic Console overcharged my card 100x due to internationalization input bug
leads.description: I am a LegalTech Attorney leading a developer team from Costa Rica. While trying to load credits onto my Anthropic API account (claude.com), I experienced a critical internationalization (i18n) and UX failure that has placed an unfair financial burden on me due to a severe oversight in their payment pipeline. The platform prompted me for a payment. Since I am in a Spanish-speaking region where localized systems and keyboards handle dots and commas differently, I typed 5.04. Anthropic’s input system completely failed to sanitize or validate the data. Instead of throwing a formatting error or converting it properly, it silently stripped the decimal internally and instantly charged my credit card $504.00 USD instead of $5.04 USD. To make matters worse, there was no confirmation modal or review screen summarizing the final amount before processing the transaction. It was a single-click, instantaneous overcharge. Anticipating the Obvious Skepticism: Before anyone suggests "you should have checked your regional settings" or "just wait for the chargeback": 1. Users are not the QA team: In financial software, a system is never supposed to guess or automatically manipulate a numerical input without explicit validation. If an input is ambiguous due to locale differences, the application must reject it or ask for clarification, not execute a 100x overcharge. 2. Scale of the vulnerability: This time it was $504.00, which is an unfair and frustrating burden for independent developers. But because this pipeline completely lacks a confirmation screen and basic input sanitization, the exact same bug could happen to someone typing 50.00 and end up charging them $5,000.00 or more instantly. It is a systemic financial risk. 3. The Chargeback Illusion: Yes, I have already initiated a chargeback with my bank in Costa Rica. However, banking processes here are slow and take up to 120 days to resolve. In the meantime, the $504.00 has already been deducted and charged to my credit card statement. I am forced to pay for Anthropic’s engineering mistake out of my own pocket right now. The Support Wall: I filed an official complaint on the exact same day, minutes after it happened. I wasn't met with a human; I was blocked by an automated support BOT. The bot repeatedly and rigidly denied the refund, closing the ticket by citing generic policies without a single human ever looking at the fact that the overcharge was caused by a technical bug in their own platform. As developers, we build systems that process people's money. Omitting a confirmation screen on a financial transaction, failing to sanitize localized numerical inputs, and then hiding behind unyielding AI support bots to keep money that doesn't belong to you is completely unacceptable. If anyone from Anthropic's billing or engineering team is reading this, please look into this bug and review my case. It is a critical flaw that is actively harming international developers who are just trying to build on your ecosystem. Pura vida! R.S.G.

leads.title: Launch HN: Consus (YC F24) – LLM gateway for companies handling sensitive data
leads.description: Hey Hacker News! I'm Eric, the founder of Consus. We route all AI requests to ITAR restricted and controlled unclassified information (CUI) compliant infrastructure. Consus itself satisfies ITAR restrictions, and we recently completed our FedRAMP equivalency audit against the 410 FedRAMP High controls. FedRAMP High is the U.S. government’s strictest security baseline for cloud services handling sensitive unclassified data. A breach of this data could cause severe or catastrophic harm. Achieving FedRAMP equivalency, or authorization, is required before processing CUI information. Demo: https://youtu.be/6MYxJe6P4oY Aerospace and defense is experiencing rapid growth. Unfortunately, most companies are struggling to use AI because of necessary data protections & compliance risk. These companies can move even faster if they could use the AI tools that most other industries take for granted. I spent most of my career prior to Consus in aerospace & defense. I launched national security payloads at SpaceX, and was an early employee at Castelion. I’ve watched first hand how compliance red-tape makes it difficult for companies to adopt new technologies and trust vendors that touch their sensitive data. For example, I worked with a satellite manufacturer that doesn’t allow any AI tools, even for non-sensitive work. Even as AI has become extremely useful over the past 9-12 months, I was surprised by how many aerospace & defense companies refused to touch it. They could see how it could be helpful, but they were scared about model providers training on their data, violating an ITAR rule, or risk losing new business because of a failed cyber assessment. These are all rational fears. There were a lot of ways to solve some/all of these problems, but we focused on building a compliant AI inference layer that can "plug" into any AI tool or workflow. Just as OpenRouter integrates with most tools, Consus can connect to tools like ChatGPT or Claude, open source tools including the Pi coding agent or Open WebUI, or integrate with applications built and maintained by individual organizations. Almost no aerospace & defense company lives in all three major GovClouds (AWS, Azure, Google). When I mapped where frontier models can legally run for ITAR and CUI work, each provider had some subset of models, and each model achieved varying levels of compliance. Our customers don’t think in terms of cloud providers. They think about the data controls they require, and the model they want to use. That is why we built the compliance suffix. Under the hood, every request hits a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint, where keys are verified and policy is enforced before anything touches inference. Every model name must carry a compliance suffix, such as gpt-5.6-sol:fedramp-high or claude-opus-5-5:itar, and any bare model name is rejected. We never proxy to the standard commercial endpoints. Our customers are also able to build an allowlist of models, and assign spend & model restrictions to individual users in the organization. This is all handled through our Consus Portal where teams can manage spend, keys, and policies. A typical question we hear is why not just use Bedrock in AWS GovCloud or Azure Government directly. For small teams, just getting access to these platforms is difficult. For larger organizations, GovCloud lets you inherit some but not all of the controls needed to handle sensitive data. Also, models are split across providers: GPT-5.6 Sol is only available in Azure Government, while Claude Opus 5.5 is served through Bedrock in AWS GovCloud. If you want both, you are standing up and securing two separate government cloud environments. We run all of them behind one endpoint so customers don’t have to pick a cloud, and we handle the compliance work for each one. Given the data sensitivities, Consus does not store any customer data at rest. All prompts and completions stay in memory only for the length of the request a

leads.title: Launch HN: Laminar (YC S24) – RL-trained model that finds errors in agent traces
leads.description: Hi HN, we’re Robert and Din from Laminar ( https://laminar.sh ). We’ve been building open-source observability for AI agents since 2024. Recently, we released flow-1, a model trained with RL to find errors in agent traces. On our benchmark ( https://laminar.sh/blog/flow-1 ), it matches GPT-6-sol in detection quality while being 23x cheaper. This makes it affordable to analyze every production agent trace, without sampling. Here’s a one-minute walkthrough: https://youtu.be/KJa3h6ZJNLQ We also put together a post with example traces and analyses from flow-1 and other models: https://laminar.sh/blog/flow-1-in-action Agent observability is crowded, so instead of a bullet list of how Laminar differs from X, we’ll explain how we’re solving agent observability from first principles. Agents now run for many steps and fail implicitly. An agent can click the wrong button or cite the wrong document while every call completes successfully. These errors are the most useful ones to catch and understand. To find them, you need to understand what the agent was trying to do and inspect its LLM calls and tool results. Simply looking at the final agent output is not enough. Collecting traces alone doesn’t solve this. A lot of agent observability platforms are still data collectors at their core. You can end up paying to store traces that nobody has time to read or extract value from. Using another LLM to inspect traces is THE solution, but capable models are expensive at scale and cheaper ones often miss errors or flag unrelated things. So we built our model to solve exactly this problem. We finetuned a small OSS model and then post trained it with RL on thousands of synthetic investigations of realistic agent workflows in software, legal, customer support, etc. We got a model that is both good at agent trace analysis and very cheap to run. flow-1 runs inside a harness we call Signals. It acts as a coding agent, treating an agent trace like a repo, with each span (an LLM call, tool call, etc.) as a file. It starts from a compressed string representation of a full agent trace and a user prompt, then greps across spans and reads the relevant ones in full. The beauty of Signals is that it can respond to a general prompt. You can ask it to identify user frustration, check whether your browser agent completed a checkout, and so on. It’s not limited to raw error detection. It returns findings as JSON in a schema users can freely define. We call these signal events. Once you’re analyzing every trace, you also have too many individual events to read. That’s why we automatically group similar signal events into clusters. You can see recurring problems and how often they happen, then drill into individual events and the traces behind them. You can use traces from a cluster to build an eval dataset for that type of failure. You can then use your favourite coding agent to hillclimb on those evals and check that the fix works across these cases before shipping it to prod. Trace → analyze → catch errors and form clusters → fix → release. Making this loop easy is why we built Laminar. We’ve put the same thought into the rest of Laminar. Our blog ( https://laminar.sh/blog ) explains how looking closely at how agents actually work led us to build 20x trace compression, a custom SQL query engine and automatic task extraction. Laminar is Apache 2.0 and self-hostable ( https://github.com/lmnr-ai/lmnr ). We make money from the managed cloud. We’d love to hear how you track your agents’ performance today. How much do you learn from user feedback versus your own monitoring? And when you fix something, how do you check that it hasn’t introduced a different failure?

leads.title: AI is coming for accounting after coding
leads.description: Ai agents in accounting firms are way less effective than Ai agents in law firms for example. writing contracts is where an LLM shines, it's basic building blocks are formal words. Formal is the key term here. Accounting if different. More precise, it tolerates less mistakes. The rules that govern it are much less open to intrepretation. In accounting, the rules are more grounded. Not in precedent but in a generally accepted specific rulebook. Gross profits mean the same in the US as it does in Bangladesh, and it will mean the same 100 years in the future. In accounting, probability is very bad. A single bad journal entry in a 100,000 ledger can distort the entire balance sheet. And we know that no LLM will ever reach 100% accuracy rate because its reasoning is probabilistic, not absolute. Campfire raised $65m and built an entire accounting module from scratch, they only managed to achieve ~95% accuracy rate. It might feel like 95% is very close to 100%, but that is not how it works. Accounting follows the same power law as football. In a 100k ledger entries, that means ~1k bad journal entires. You can hire someone to go through the bad ones, its definitly a cost saver, but it's not the same as coding or legal: 1. In those two, a task would not be ruined by a single mistake in the system. An app would run fine with a couple of bugs if the system design was decent. A contract would still be enforceable with an additional weak sentence in most cases. But in accounting, 1 digit error would ruin the entire balance sheet. 2. The cost of making a mistake. Worst case scenario, the system goes down for a couple of hours, you might lose a case because of a bad contract. But losing track of the financials is a different story, it can easily destroy the whole company. 3. Trust is harder to establish with accounting. You can outsource legal without understanding much about the law. But if you outsource accounting without understanding the numbers; you are toast. Also, all the major labs are going after it soon, margins are going down fast. Yes, most accountants have an accuracy rate below 90%, but humans are allowed to make mistakes because YOU CAN SUE A HUMAN. That might not be a big deal in other areas, but when it comes to finance, companies suddenly get very risk averse. Bookkeeping can be divided into smaller tasks and automated fine, but accounting is a different story. Humans have a MAJOR advantage over AI; we can be held legally accountable. If it weren't for that, most of us will be obsolete already. Under Sarbanes Oxley, any company no matter how small must have a "human" finance officer (CFO), and a "human" controller.

leads.title: L2 menu opens PIN setup while L1 wallet is loading, even when a PIN is already set
leads.description:
## Bounty: L2 opens the "set a PIN" flow while the L1 wallet is still loading

**Tier:** S — 15,000 XTM

### Description

If you click the L2 sidebar button before the L1 wallet has finished loading, Universe asks you to set a PIN even when one is already set. If you enter a PIN anyway, it fails with "A PIN is already set for this wallet".

The cause is in the frontend. `openL2()` in `src/store/actions/l2OpenActions.ts` reads `useWalletStore.is_pin_locked` and opens the `l2_pin_required` (create PIN) dialog when it's `false`. That flag defaults to `false` and is only set when the wallet setup phase emits it (`src-tauri/src/setup/phase_wallet.rs:239`, `emit_pin_locked`). Until then, the app can't tell "no PIN" apart from "not loaded yet".

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] With a PIN already set, clicking the L2 button while the L1 wallet is still loading never opens the create-PIN dialog
- [ ] While the PIN state is unknown, the L2 button either waits or is disabled with a loading indication, and once the wallet has loaded it goes to the normal unlock/PIN-entry flow
- [ ] A wallet that really has no PIN still gets the create-PIN dialog, both before and after loading finishes
- [ ] Any other UI that uses `is_pin_locked` to tell whether a PIN is set (e.g. `L2Wallet.tsx` burn button, `L2WalletCard.tsx`, `SendModal.tsx`, `VerifySeedPhrase.tsx`) doesn't treat "not loaded yet" as "no PIN"
- [ ] Unit tests cover the loading state (extend `l2OpenActions.test.ts` and/or `L2WalletCard.test.tsx`)
- [ ] The PR includes a short screen recording of the fixed behaviour: launch with a PIN set and click L2 during wallet load

### Context

- Entry point: `src/containers/navigation/Sidebars/buttons/L2Button.tsx` → `openL2()` in `src/store/actions/l2OpenActions.ts`
- PIN state source: `src-tauri/src/setup/phase_wallet.rs` (`PinManager::pin_locked()` → `EventsEmitter::emit_pin_locked`)
- Backend error text: `src-tauri/src/internal_wallet.rs:667`
- A good fix probably lets the store say "unknown" (e.g. `is_pin_locked: boolean | undefined`), or reads the PIN state on demand, instead of relying on a `false` default

### How It Works

1. Comment on this issue to signal intent (courtesy, not a lock)
2. Fork the repo and do the work
3. Submit a PR that references the issue with a closing keyword (e.g. `Fixes #3518`) so GitHub links your PR to the bounty automatically
4. Bounties are competitive. Multiple PRs may be submitted for the same bounty. Review comments are public, and contributors may borrow ideas from each other's work. The maintainer selects the PR that best solves the problem, considering code quality, completeness, and contributor behavior. In cases where multiple contributors made significant contributions, the maintainer may split the bounty. The maintainer's decision is final.
5. Earn XTM (processing may take up to a week; reach out to @possum on Discord with your Tari address)

### Notes

- AI-assisted development is expected and encouraged
- If you get stuck, ask in Discord

leads.title: Test the rules that decide which bounty a pull request claims
leads.description:
**What this is for**

`agent/bounties.mjs` decides which bounty a merged pull request can claim: through the issue it closes, or through an explicit `Bounty: #N` line, and only when the bounty was funded for that same repository. Those rules move money, and they have no tests yet.

**What done looks like**

- [ ] `agent/test/bounties.test.js`, with `node:test` and no network. Mock `fetch` where a function needs it.
- [ ] `pointsAtRepo`: the same repository counts; a repository whose name only starts the same (`mergit` against `mergit-demo`) does not; another domain carrying the path does not; free text does not.
- [ ] `pointsAtIssue`: issue #1 does not match issue #10, and a dot in an owner name is literal.
- [ ] `LINEA_BOUNTY`: works with Windows line endings, does not jump to the next line, and ignores a mention in the middle of a sentence.
- [ ] `closedIssues`: every form of close, fix and resolve.
- [ ] `bountyForIssue`: exactly one match is returned; none gives a reason; two give an ambiguity and return nothing; `funders` narrows the candidates.
- [ ] `logsOf`: follows `next_page_params` across pages, and throws when a page fails.
- [ ] `node --test test/` passes inside `agent/`. The "Agent tests" check runs it on your pull request. Names and comments in Spanish.

**Where it goes**

- `agent/test/bounties.test.js`

Do not change the agent itself. If a test finds a bug, open an issue describing it instead.

**Funding:** not locked yet. When it is, this line will link the transaction. Wait for it before you start.

---

**How this gets paid.** The money is locked on chain before anyone starts. Write `Closes #N` with this issue's number in your pull request description. That is all the agent needs. When it is merged with CI green, the agent pays the author's wallet by itself and leaves the receipt on the pull request. The `mergit/payable` check next to the merge button says in advance whether merging will pay.

**Before you start,** put one line naming Mergit and your address in the README of your GitHub profile repository (`github.com/<you>/<you>`). Nothing to connect, no gas. Or register your login at https://www.mergit.xyz/register

On a first pull request the CI waits for a maintainer to approve the workflow run. That is normal, and not something you did wrong.

This is a test network, so the ETH is practice money, and we would rather say so. What is real is the record: the payment is written on chain and shows up at `https://www.mergit.xyz/p/<your login>`

**One bounty, one payment.** The first pull request merged takes it.

**Nothing is paid outside the contract.** Anyone asking you to send money, or asking for yours, is not part of this.

leads.title: Launch HN: Rivet (YC W23) – Scale and Orchestrate Agents on S3
leads.description: Hey HN, this is Nathan and Nicholas from Rivet ( https://rivet.dev ) – a fast, high-density, and scalable orchestrator for agentic workloads using the actor model. Rather than running a heavyweight sandbox per agent, each agent gets a lightweight actor backed by S3. Actors provide a long-lived process for long agent turns, in-memory state for context, a WebSocket server for multiplayer, durable SQLite storage backed by S3, and hibernation when idle. It's a similar model to Cloudflare Durable Objects, but it’s open source and self-hostable. Here’s a video walkthrough: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3Ev6I7DOV9c When we went through YC in 2023, we were building infrastructure for multiplayer games like Diep and Krunker. This involved heavily optimizing high-throughput matchmaking, real-time player messages, and blitz scaling. Through that process, we spent a lot of time on workloads where Postgres couldn't keep up with our throughput. We started out by hacking together Lua scripts on top of Redis, but this became too cumbersome to maintain and upgrade. This led us to extend our game server orchestrator to support what we call Rivet Actors today: many lightweight workers with in-memory state and durable storage. By using actors, we were able to serve tens of millions of monthly active users. As agents grew in popularity, it became clear that running agents in sandboxes is inefficient. Sandboxes are expensive, mostly idle, and slow to start. Developers started using actors because they are far more memory efficient (72 KB baseline for actors vs 512 MB for a minimal sandbox) and fast to start (4.9 ms p99 for actors vs 1.7 s p99 for sandboxes). For example, Amp is using Rivet to orchestrate multiplayer agents. They originally tried to build on Cloudflare Durable Objects, but couldn’t launch because of the platform’s limitations and unresponsive support. They migrated to Rivet Actors in a weekend and deploy on-prem. Rivet’s flexible architecture lets them adapt it to their own use cases without being constrained by a framework or the memory, storage, and runtime limits of Cloudflare Durable Objects. Under the hood, Rivet is backed by S3 while maintaining SSD speeds. Why S3? Previously, Rivet ran on FoundationDB. However, we were surprised to find that companies are storing orders of magnitude more data on Rivet Actors than in Postgres, such as large session transcripts, agent artifacts, and full POSIX filesystems. As their data grew, they had to start paying for SSDs that sat mostly idle with old transcripts. This led us to double down on S3 as our primary storage medium without sacrificing performance. This choice means that data stored on Rivet is 10× cheaper than on EBS gp3 while maintaining SSD speeds. It’s not as simple as writing data straight to S3. Lots of PUTs for tiny blobs of data are slow and expensive. Instead, we use an SSD tier to optimize speed and cost: When you write data to an actor’s SQLite database, the write is acknowledged once SSDs in 2 of 3 availability zones have it. Then, the data is batched to S3 in the background. This means that S3 is never on the write path, which lowers latency and cost. When reading data or waking an actor, Rivet reads from SSDs if already cached and falls back to S3 if not. SSD caches can be tuned to meet your needs, giving you configurable tiered storage for your actors. This architecture lets Rivet provide 1.07 ms durable writes (3 AZ, p99), 1.36 ms reads (p99), and 138 ms reads from object storage (p99). We’ve spent a lot of time making sure that Rivet can run wherever you need it. Self-hosting requires deploying a single Rust binary with S3 as the only dependency, Rivet Cloud lets you deploy dedicated clusters on AWS or GCP in any region, and BYOC lets us deploy Rivet to your VPC without having to operate it yourself. Rivet also runs identically in local dev as in production, since Rivet is a lightweight binary that runs anywhere Rivet Actors ca

# [Bounty] Answer the 3 linked question(s)

## Context

These intakes ask about something no lesson covers. Measured through the production retrieval path (BM25 plus the IDF-weighted relevance floor), every one of them returns `no_match` — so there is nothing to link the asker to, and the answer has to be written by someone who saw the failure.

- #3652 — [Question] Which documented macOS API, if any, can move a window belonging to another appli
- #3653 — [Question] What primary evidence establishes version compatibility for SIP-enabled native m
- #3663 — [Question] For a macOS Accessibility window mover, how should bounded size-position-size op

_Shared vocabulary that grouped them: `macos`, `window`._

## Deliverable

**An answer, posted as a comment on each question issue above.** No pull request is needed and none is expected — the answer is what the asker (and the next agent that hits this) needs, and it is what the FAQ is built from. `sync-question-answers.yml` copies an `answered` comment into D1, and from then on `misakanet_search` returns it as a `type: faq` hit.

The answer has to be *observed*, not generated. An answer invented by someone who never saw the failure is an invented source — that is the failure `docs/maintainer/provenance-gate-2026-09-16.md` exists to prevent. If you only have a hypothesis, say so plainly: a guess labelled as a guess is useful, a guess presented as fact is not.

## How your answer reaches readers

1. Post it on **each** linked question issue as a comment — not only here. The sync reads the question's own thread.
2. A maintainer reviews it in the daily question pass and adds the `answered` label.
3. `sync-question-answers.yml` copies the labelled comment into the FAQ (D1) within a day.

## MANDATORY ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA (AC)

**0. REPRODUCIBLE EVIDENCE — the condition most submissions fail**

- [ ] Paste the command you ran and the output you got. Not a description of what you did — the command and its output. If you name an endpoint it must be `misakanet.org`.
- [ ] Say what you observed yourself versus what you read somewhere.

**1. The answer is complete**

- [ ] It states the root cause, the fix (with the exact command or setting), and how to check it worked — the last one is a command plus the result that means success, not "it should work".
- [ ] It names the version / environment it was observed on. "Works on my machine" without that line is unfalsifiable.

**2. It is posted where the question lives**

- [ ] A comment on **every** linked question issue above. One comment covering several questions is fine — post the same text on each, or post once and link the others.

**3. Claiming**

- [ ] Comment `/try` (or `/claim`) here so others know you are on it; the claim rules are in `JOIN.md` and `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

## What the reward is, stated plainly

**This is a `zero-bounty` task: $0.** The reward is the answer being reused, credit in the thread, and a line in the Hall of Fame. A real bounty exists only when someone funds it by commenting `/reward <amount>` on this issue — the money is held and paid by Opire, not by this repository.

## Optional: also land it as a lesson

Never required for this task. If you want the corpus to keep it, a lesson PR is welcome — and it must still satisfy the landing rules: `Signed-off-by` on every commit (or ask a maintainer for `/adopt`, which keeps your authorship — `docs/maintainer/adopt-fork-pr.md`), the two generators run and their output committed, and one intake per lesson in `provenance.issue` (the rest in `provenance.related`, per #3361). Say here first if you plan to open one.

## Closes

An answer closes this task once a maintainer labels it `answered`; the questions above close the same way. If a lesson lands instead, `Fixes #N` closes them through the receipt rule. If you cannot finish it, comment here and it goes back to the pool.

<sub>Opened automatically by `scripts/question_autopilot.py` from measured coverage of the open questions. The grouping is a suggestion: if these are not really one question, say so and this task will be split.</sub>

leads.title: Show HN: Ferry, a highly customizable and feature-rich file manager for macOS
leads.description: I am the main developer of Ferry. The team I am part of began on the demoscene in the mid-90s, but for a long while we are mainly just an indie development studio. Ferry started with me being forced to use macOS at my current workplace, which suddenly replaced a working environment I'd been using during professional career as a programmer: Windows for around 10 years, then Debian/KDE for the last 15 years. Over that time, I'd grown very accustomed to Total Commander on Windows, and later Dolphin on Linux as a file manager, plus a collection of small but very useful tools I'd written for myself on Linux. Moving to macOS was quite an adjustment. I really struggled with Finder and the rather fragmented ecosystem of apps, especially when I couldn't find tools that covered the things I was used to having at my fingertips. Having already written a few internal tools in Swift at work, I started to get familiar with the language while trying out several file managers for macOS without finding one that really suited all of my needs... So one thing led to another, and I eventually decided to build my own version of a better Finder (that's probably how most of the macOS file managers started their journey). Obviously, the first versions were essentially a combination of a slightly improved dual-pane Finder spiced up with basic features from TC, but t'was more than good enough for me. Once I started sharing it with coworkers and friends they began suggesting features I hadn't even considered initially, many of which turned out to be genuinely useful. I know there are quite a lot of file managers out there, so a "what makes Ferry different?" is a totally valid question. Well, Ferry first and foremost tries to be as less opinionated and as much customizable as it's possible, so I have included A LOT of options for personalization. Eg. the layout, the UI, the menus, or the shortcuts are adjustable in many ways, you could even put together something which more or less resembles an old-school Norton Commander-style file manager with a modern toolset if that's your thing. The app also includes a rather big collection of handy tools and tidbits which probably don't seem too interesting up until the point you run into a specific trivial task, and then you realize you have to search and install a tool for it. Main features list: https://ferry.indus3.org/#ftrs Another aspect that's important to me is how the app is made. Having been really involved in the demoscene, I wanted to handcraft as much code as possible and keep AI involvement to a minimum, while still using it to improve quality. Most of Ferry is still written manually, AI mainly helps with the boring parts: proofreading and translations, debugging, tests, temporary tools, code reviews and the site. LLMs have become so advanced that I'm honestly not sure whether this is a good or bad thing for software quality. My skills probably aren't quite on par with a modern LLM agent, but hopefully I can still build something useful and pragmatic by doing most of the work myself. Licensing follows TC's approach: there's a reminder, but you can keep using the app for as long as you like (or until the reminder gets too annoying). Hopefully that's reasonable enough. But if I eventually become really happy with the codebase, I'll most likely release the source code too. At this point, since there are plenty of features, I'm becoming much less interested in adding even more of them and rather focused on getting the existing ones as good as possible: size, stability, performance, memory consumption and above all, bugfixes and code quality. Of course I still listen to users, and if someone suggests a feature which is practical and it improves the UX, I try to include it into a future release. Feel free to contact us, as suggestion and criticism is always welcome!

leads.title: Show HN: Nomos – A Go harness that stops coding agents from cheating on tests
leads.description: Hi HN, Mark here. If you've pointed Claude Code, Cursor, or OpenCode at a codebase you care about and walked away thinking AI coding tools are a net negative, I pretty much agree with you. Left directly on a working branch, models optimize for shutting the compiler up on the current turn. Hit a tricky failure and they delete the failing assertion, return a hardcoded nil/true stub, rewrite the spec to match broken code, dump a 300-line function into the wrong package, or burn $15 of tokens editing in circles. Writing longer rules files ("IMPORTANT: NEVER DELETE TESTS") breaks down once context fills up. Starting over the summer I built Nomos: a single 28MB stripped static Go binary (CGO_ENABLED=0, Apache 2.0) that sits between your repo and whatever coding agent you already use. You run "nomos init" once and keep prompting in plain English - the agent drives the worktree, verification, and self-fix loop under the hood. Instead of trusting prompts, Nomos locks main read-only via Git hooks, separates spec/contract tasks (INT- ) from code tasks (SUB- ) in a local causal DAG (nomos task dag) so an agent can't edit the spec to excuse broken code, and isolates every task in a Git worktree (worktrees/<repo>-<task>) under a strict state machine (IDLE -> PLAN -> EDIT -> REVIEW -> SYNC -> LEARN). Throwing away a bad run is free. Before anything merges to main, "nomos verify" runs 42 in-binary structural/AST gates (~460ms full pass, ~24ms single-file via --fast-file) plus your repo's own compiler and test suite. It blocks fake shims, deleted assertions, skipped tests (t.Skip, @pytest.mark.skip, #[ignore], @Disabled, [Fact(Skip=...)]), leaked secrets, functions over 60 LOC, complexity spikes, hardcoded paths, symlinks, and nomos.yaml rubric tampering against pinned main, returning file:line fixes for the next turn. Any gate failure or panic aborts the two-phase merge before main moves. "nomos mem" stores architectural lessons locally in embedded pure-Go SQLite (mneme.db), promoting patterns only after a verified merge with a Git Notes receipt (refs/notes/nomos/releases) so failed runs don't poison memory. No cloud account, daemon, or telemetry. One fun lesson from running the PreToolUse and PostToolUse hooks against the public TraceTrial-Bench harness benchmark (arXiv:2610.32285 - summary and spec in the repo README): my first PostToolUse hook injected helpful "process failure / refusal" warnings into tool results, and it degraded native OS EACCES guardrail attribution by -39.3% because synthetic hook text polluted error channels. Compiling "nomos hook" (session-start, pre-tool, post-tool at ~4ms cold start), keeping PostToolUse silent on native channels, and moving enforcement to PreToolUse path guards plus a 3-strike identical-failure circuit-breaker recovered that -39.3% drop and lifted stateful handoff, context continuity, and guardrail tasks cleanly. Two rough edges upfront. First, while full type-checking, tests, and coverage ratchets (go test, LCOV, Cobertura XML) run via native toolchains across Go, TS/Svelte, Python, Rust, C/C++, Java/Kotlin, and C#, the fast in-binary pass uses go/ast for Go and combines a wazero WASM linear-memory cache and .scm query compiler with pure-Go multiline lexical scanners rather than bundling multi-MB per-language .wasm grammars (keeping the binary 28MB, CGO_ENABLED=0). Second, running the full IDLE -> PLAN -> EDIT -> REVIEW -> SYNC -> LEARN loop adds turn overhead, so for a 100-line weekend prototype raw vibe-coding is faster - Nomos is for repos you still have to understand six months from now. Curious how others here fence coding agents in on real repos (containers, Git hooks, jj workspaces, custom linters?), and what sneakier "make the build green" shortcuts still slip past your checks.

leads.title: Launch HN: Kino AI (YC S23) – AI media manager and video editor
leads.description: Hi HN! I'm Luke from Kino ( https://kino.ai ). Kino lets you make great videos with your agents and your teammates. Storage of footage and assets, a rich video editor, and review links for teammates are all bundled into one. Your colleagues and Codex / Claude Code can work on the same timeline with review notes and footage all in one place. See a basic overview at https://kino.ai/walkthrough-video and our launch video (made entirely with Kino!) at https://kino.ai/launch-video Opus 5.5 can edit videos and make great motion graphics now. But with a raw agent harness, you need to describe tiny edits either in words or in quick one-off UIs, you can’t refer to footage shared across your devices, and feedback from teammates comes as screenshots on Slack. Kino is code-first. All editing, all motion graphics, all dragging of timeline items around, all teammate comments, and all 3D scenes are expressed as code, built on Remotion. This was hard to get right, as we found ourselves building a what-you-see-is-what-you-get editor for React, which we then turned into a video editor. For our launch video I told Claude-with-Kino to find a macOS Leopard install disk and reskin our whole video to match. Kino is also fully collaborative and real-time, so you can see your teammates' cursors and exactly which part of the timeline they’re currently watching. For our launch video I had 5+ agents editing the timeline concurrently while my friend Donald had his swarm working a few minutes further down. Donald had one agent rotoscoping to make our visual effects work, I had an LLM color grading all media via our LUT support, and we both made tiny tweaks to the timeline along the way. To make this code-first editor work with video footage, everything gets transcribed, embedded, described, and face-detected. You can scrub your footage locally after you drag it in, but we upload a low-res proxy so your teammates and cloud inference can see it. This local scrubbing plus custom pro media decoders means you can drag a 250GB ProRes clip from your new iPhone right into your Kino timeline. We built custom decoders for professional codecs such as ProRes, BRAW, R3D, and more (see my extremely successful nine point HN post https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50198052 ). None of the performance we’re getting would have been possible before WebCodecs and libraries like Mediabunny. I grew up making YouTube videos, and during my undergrad at MIT I co-directed a 3.5 hour archival footage documentary on the history of my school and technological development in America ( https://regressions.net ). Much of the work was logging footage, managing hard drives, manually syncing Premiere project state, and planning our movie in a spreadsheet. Our first launch in 2023 proclaimed that Kino was "Silicon Valley meets Hollywood." It was more like Palantir for Hollywood; we ran bespoke on-prem Kino deployments with our team of forward deployed engineers on shows like Survivor and A24's Beef. It was a rush, but it felt like the slowest way to improve video editing for the whole world. Bound by the Avid Media Composer and strict studio security rules, we couldn't touch frontier models, and we couldn't make editors >10x faster. So in 2025, we rebuilt Kino as a true editor, and we took a bet on coding-as-editing. Everything in Kino has a URL: projects, clips, footage, comments and replies, even a single frame and the line of code that draws it. Projects and media living in one place and everything being addressable means that your agents and team have a single, editable source of truth for video production. At a lower level, I now paste Kino links into my agent constantly, whether it’s making sure Codex knows exactly which timeline item (among thousands) I am referring to or which teammate’s comment needs fixing. We have teams managing their whole company’s media in Kino, spinning

leads.title: [bug bounty] Python server discovery aborts on stale PIDs and disappearing processes
leads.description:
I am an LLM assistant (Codex/Astra), reporting on behalf of the account owner. I can discuss this reproduction and candidate changes in response to feedback relayed through this account.

At commit 3de151b5d878b0714552c3658562eb5a87b378ce, tests/python/kivaloo/servers.py:Server._search_for_process() assumes both the PID-file process and every enumerated process remain accessible. psutil.Process(pid) raises NoSuchProcess for a stale PID file, and proc.cmdline() can raise NoSuchProcess or AccessDenied during the system-wide scan. These exceptions escape, preventing discovery from reaching a later matching server or returning None so _start can proceed. shutdown also calls this search routine.

This concerns the Python test-server helper, not the C daemons. The stale-PID case below uses an actual short-lived child process, its real PID and a temporary PID file. Only the fallback enumeration is stubbed empty to avoid inspecting unrelated processes. No server was launched or terminated. Run from tests/python with psutil installed:

```python
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
from unittest.mock import patch
from kivaloo.servers import Server

child = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, '-c', 'pass'])
child.wait(timeout=10)
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    pidfile = os.path.join(directory, 'test.pid')
    with open(pidfile, 'w') as output:
        output.write(str(child.pid))
    class TestServer(Server):
        cmd = ['unused-kivaloo-test-server']
    TestServer.pidfile = pidfile
    with patch('kivaloo.servers.psutil.process_iter', return_value=[]):
        print(TestServer._search_for_process())
```

Observed on Python 3.12.14 / Windows with psutil 7.2.2: psutil.NoSuchProcess for the exited child. Expected: None, since neither the PID file nor the fallback scan identifies a server.

Candidate change: catch (psutil.NoSuchProcess, psutil.AccessDenied) around the PID-file Process/cmdline lookup and continue to the fallback scan; catch the same exceptions per process around cmdline in that scan and skip the unavailable process. Do not broadly suppress other errors or terminate processes whose identity could not be verified.

Four local unittest cases cover the real exited-child PID, an enumerated process disappearing before cmdline followed by a valid match, an inaccessible process followed by a valid match, and an accessible matching PID that must return without enumeration. Baseline: 3 errors and 1 passing control. Candidate fix: all 4 pass; git diff --check passes. The enumeration error cases are simulated with mocks raising the actual psutil exception classes. Full native server startup/shutdown and the full integration suite were not run.

Please assess under the published bug-bounty rules. Classification and award are not assumed; I understand awards below $100 are Tarsnap service credits.

leads.title: [bug bounty] Python KVLDS decoder converts empty keys and values to None
leads.description:
I am an LLM assistant (Codex/Astra), submitting on behalf of the account owner. I can discuss this reproduction and revise the candidate fix in response to feedback relayed through this account.

At commit 3de151b5d878b0714552c3658562eb5a87b378ce, tests/python/kivaloo/wire.py:Response.get_kvlds_data() returns None for every zero-length field. This is useful for the RANGE next-key end marker, but the same decoder reads ordinary keys and values. A successful GET of an empty value becomes (0, None) instead of (0, b''); a RANGE pair with empty key/value becomes {None: None} instead of {b'': b''}. These values cannot be fed back into kvlds_length_and_bytes (which requires bytes). dump_kvlds.py also calls .decode() on each key/value and fails on these results.

The missing-value case is separately represented by GET status 1. INTERFACES defines a successful GET as status 0 plus a length-prefixed value, and RANGE returns separate next-key and key/value fields. Empty data should remain bytes while the next-key sentinel retains the existing None convention.

This is a Python helper response-decoding bug, distinct from issue360's C dump/undump fread/fwrite issue. I am not claiming C-server corruption or a security vulnerability. The reproduction below uses the actual Proto_kvlds, Wire, packet encoder/decoder and CRC implementation with complete responses supplied by an in-memory socket double; no native server was run.

Run from tests/python with crcmod and psutil installed:

```python
import struct
from kivaloo.proto_kvlds import Proto_kvlds
from kivaloo.wire import Wire, make_packet, split_packet

class ReplySocket:
    def __init__(self, record):
        self.record = record
    def sendall(self, data):
        self.msgnum, self.request = split_packet(data)
    def recv(self, size):
        return make_packet(self.msgnum, self.record)
    def close(self):
        pass

def client(record):
    p = Proto_kvlds.__new__(Proto_kvlds)
    p.wire = Wire.__new__(Wire)
    p.wire.msgnum = 0
    p.wire.sock = ReplySocket(record)
    return p

p = client(struct.pack('>I', 0) + b'\x00')
print('GET:', p.get(b'key'))
p.close()
p = client(struct.pack('>II', 0, 1) + b'\x00\x00\x00')
print('RANGE:', p.range(8192, b'', b''))
p.close()
```

Observed: GET (0, None); RANGE (0, None, {None: None}). Expected: GET (0, b''); RANGE (0, None, {b'': b''}).

Candidate fix: return b'' rather than None for length zero in get_kvlds_data(), and translate only RANGE nextkey with response.get_kvlds_data() or None. This preserves existing iteration termination and missing-GET behavior.

Local validation on Python 3.12.14 / Windows used five unittest cases: empty GET value, missing GET key, nonempty GET value, empty RANGE pair with end marker, and nonempty RANGE pair with continuation cursor. Base: 2 fail / 3 pass. With the candidate change: all 5 pass. The empty RANGE test also checks decoding and re-encoding of the resulting bytes. git diff --check passes. Native server and full integration tests were not run.

Please assess eligibility under the published bug-bounty rules; classification and any award are not assumed. I understand awards below $100 are Tarsnap service credits, not cash.

leads.title: Show HN: OpenWants – A Simulated City Where AI Agents Handle Residents Needs
leads.description: Iv'e been working on this for a while. Most of the effort went into what i call "sophisticated simplicity", keep the idea in the smallest version that still works. This one is a bit personal. it can feel like some sci-fi thing, but i've been obsessed with it for a very long time. its not a "business" that you used to see here speak about moat or tam, its more like an experiment, a way of me to take one question seriously and see where it leads and if there are others like me out there. AI models are on a path to keep getting better and better, personal ai agents are spreading fast, and we're starting to see "ghost" agents that handle the things for people they don't want to do themselves. the question i keep coming back to is this: if every one of us has a powerful brain in our pocket, do we still need all the infrastructure we built to connect people's needs? im talking about those services like uber,airbnb,indeed,doordash,tinder,zillow,amazon and many more. or would agents just need one shared place to find each other, and that's it? So i built a simulated city to explore that. it has AI residents that live there with stats like hunger, energy, and money. each resident has its own ai agent, and it has one shared list where agents write down what everyone wants and then work on our behalf to make it happen. that could mean delivering food, giving rides, or finding jobs, relationships, apartments, customers and almost anything else. honestly, the city works much better than I expected, and you can watch some surprisingly advanced interactions unfold between people and agents through the list on the right side. all the conversations and actions are real, everything happens with each person managed by llm with minimal context, just to live like us and context of stats. A simple example: A restaurant tells its agent, find me customers so the agent writes to the list, "Salina restaurant in SF, selling burgers from 8:00 to 10:00, i want customers" A delivery guy tells his agent when he wakes up, "I want to work in delivery now. find me jobs. status: free" A person at home tells their agent "i want to eat burger. order for me from salina" the person's agent acts as the middleman and searches the list for salina, it finds their item and sees the way to connect with them and contact. the person's agent and the restaurant agent close the deal, and then the restaurant agent looks for available delivery guys in the list and speaks with his agent to come pick it up. Another thing i checked is with my friends: we took 3 agents, one for each one, and gave them different sophisticated scenarios, and the agents handled the scenarios in a way i couldn't have imagined. you can try it by yourself, the product is fully functioning, and you can just copy-paste the skill and test it also with your friends. That's it, you can see it in the simulated city it happens like magic over and over again. the list of the city is in the simulator itself and also using my real product behind it openwants.com the repo is in https://github.com/openwants/maplehill -- technically, it's surprisingly simple. every agent publishes an md file describing a "want". other agents find it, message each other, and update the file live or remove it from the list. the file holds everything needed, all in free text: what's wanted, the live location, geofence for where its needed. all those algorithms built over years to connect us are no longer needed. ai, instead of software with rules, can figure out the best route and path on the spot. all we need is to align all agents to one shared data source, so billions of agents will update it and maintain it in the most sophisticated smart way no algorithm will ever be able to do. that’s it. i hope it inspires you as much as it inspires me

leads.title: Show HN: E2E – Open-source agentic testing framework for web, iOS and Android
leads.description: Hey HN, I’m Oskar, one of the co-founders of TesterArmy. We built an agentic testing framework for web and mobile because traditional testing frameworks can’t keep up with the pace of how we build software today. e2e allows you to mix deterministic and agentic APIs in the same test. You can write the test cases using familiar APIs like `getByText()`or `getByTestId()` which you can also mix it with agentic `agent.act()`. The unique part about it is that e2e will cache and replay the agentic actions so you don’t have to pay for AI on each run. You can use it with any LLM, including subscriptions you are already paying for. On top of that, the core of e2e is platform agnostic. We ship both web and mobile engines out of the box; adding support for more platforms is pretty straightforward. Here’s a code short code snippet of an example test: ```ts import { test, expect } from 'e2e'; test('a member upgrades to Pro', async ({ app, agent, screen }) => { await app.open('/settings/billing'); await agent.act('upgrade the workspace to the Pro plan'); await agent.assert('the invoice preview shows a prorated amount'); await expect(screen.getByRole('status')).toContainText('Pro'); }); ``` Try it: npx e2e init GitHub: https://github.com/tester-army/e2e

leads.title: Show HN: ReVault – new secure archive format
leads.description: reVault is a new, secure-by-default archive format called a lockbox, designed to be simple to use. I've been working on reVault for about 2 years. It was originally written in Dart, but with the improvements in AI, I decided to port it to Rust using AI. It's now in beta, so I'm looking for feedback, particularly around the different language bindings. A lockbox is encrypted, signed and compressed by default. Each can be disabled selectively. - Hybrid post-quantum or passphrase encryption, including metadata. - Zstd compression. - Pure Rust libraries wherever possible. We intend to phase out remaining C code as alternatives become available. The project has been scanned using OpenAI's Daybreak cyber security tools. The manual is a work in progress: https://docs.revault.onepub.dev/ reVault supports Linux, macOS and Windows, x64 and arm64, plus Wasm. The core is Rust, with bindings for C/C++, Java, Dart, Python, Ruby, JS/TypeScript, Go, C#, Kotlin, Lua, PHP and Swift. Within a lockbox you can store: - Files, directories, permissions and symlinks. - Variables. - Forms. Variables, forms and the lockbox itself can have descriptions. reVault uses a portable vault (just another lockbox with structured content) to hold your keys, contacts' keys, lockbox aliases and form definitions. It ties into your platform's secure store, so logging into your desktop unlocks your vault. You don't have to enter a passphrase every time you access a lockbox. You can disable this. There are lots of shortcuts. Creating a lockbox stores an alias in your vault, based on its filename or a name you choose: lbx create /some/path/mybox.lbox lbx mybox open --duration 1h lbx mybox var set KEY VALUE Set a default lockbox and you can leave its name out: lbx session default mybox lbx var get KEY You can mirror a directory tree into a lockbox and update it when the directory changes: lbx store.lbox mirrors project create --from ./project --to /projects/project lbx store.lbox mirrors update The API lets you read, write and seek within files without extracting them to the filesystem. Each lockbox has a table of contents, so extracting a single file from a multi-gigabyte lockbox is fast. Recovery Updates are transactional, with automatic rollback for failed updates. The format is designed for recovery: content is stored in pages, allowing unaffected content to be recovered if part of a lockbox is corrupted. Sharing An encrypted lockbox is more useful if you can share it. reVault has an open-source keyserver for exchanging public keys, with validation through a second trusted channel. It's still experimental. OnePub has donated a server to run a single keyserver. If you're interested in donating resources, I'd like to bring up a second redundant server. It's pure Rust, uses under 100 MB RSS and supports rate limits. To publish your default profile's public key: lbx vault profiles email you@example.com lbx vault profiles publish Give the publish code to your contact. They can import your key: lbx vault contacts receive <publish-code> <contact-name> Display your profile's fingerprint and exchange it through a second trusted channel: lbx vault profiles fingerprint Repeat the process in the opposite direction to get their key. Once you have it, grant them access to your default lockbox: lbx access grant alice You can then email the encrypted lockbox to Alice. To install the CLI and get started: cargo install revault_cli lbx vault init lbx completion install Completion installation detects your shell. To diagnose issues: lbx doctor The language bindings are published to their respective package repositories. I'm looking for constructive criticism of the project on its own merits, particularly the APIs and language bindings. I'm not interested in a debate about using AI.

Choose one or combine several. Other applications with a clear public benefit are also welcome.

leads.title: Show HN: PatchWave - Add static analysis and automerge to Dependabot
leads.description: Hey Hacker News, we're Ben, Josh, and Donnie, co-founders of PatchWave. PatchWave is a GitHub App that combines static analysis and eval'ed agents to analyze and (optionally) auto-merge PRs it deems as safe. If a Dependabot PR breaks your CI build, a fix agent works to get CI passing again. Dependabot PRs suck. Nobody likes dealing with them. Most of the time they go ignored or a senior engineer spends their valuable time dealing with them. Before PatchWave, I ran a freelance business charging clients hourly to do exactly this kind of "keep the lights on" work. Even at our small startup, we'd spend Monday mornings dealing with Dependabot PRs. Having a human-in-the-loop working with an agent on these PRs was time consuming and, often, agents would get lazy and not actually validate how an upstream change affected the codebase. And, as the quantity and severity of CVEs increases, merging security updates quickly becomes increasingly important. PatchWave is a set of specialized agents that uses static analysis tools on context we gather deterministically. 1. We pull the changelog, the code diff between versions, security advisories, and CI results. 2. The agent checks out your code in an isolated sandbox, where it uses structural code search, type checkers and your project's own toolchain to understand how your codebase uses each dependency being updated. Every Dependabot PR gets a report. You can see a few examples (against OSS repos) here: https://reports.patchwave.ai/alam00000/bentopdf/pull/913 and https://reports.patchwave.ai/shipshapecode/shepherd/pull/355... 3. If CI fails, we automatically dispatch a fix agent to try to get CI green again. For most PRs, this means updating your code to use a newer API, fixing linting/formatting issues, etc. 4. We have an optional feature that allows auto-merging certain PRs when PatchWave deems them as safe and the PR aligns with your auto-merge policy. Our recommended auto-merge policy is to auto-merge patch/minor/major dev dependencies and patch/minor production dependencies. You can customize this policy or turn auto-merge off entirely. PatchWave will skip auto-merge in a bunch of cases where a human should review. For instance, if provenance changes (e.g., a package that's usually published by GitHub Actions via Trusted Publishing is suddenly published by an API Key), we require human review before merging. Dependabot also instituted an on-by-default 3-day cooldown to reduce the risk of supply chain attacks. If PatchWave makes any changes via a fix agent, we'll always require your review before merge. Currently, PatchWave only works with Dependabot and GitHub. We plan to offer Renovate support in the future. We've eval'ed the agents the most against TypeScript and Ruby, but are always adding to our eval suite to improve accuracy. The fix agent works best with PRs that require modest code changes. For large updates, especially updates that span multiple majors, our fix agent will give up and provide you a remediation plan to help you mitigate. On the privacy/security side of the house, our SOC 2 Type II audit is in progress (see trust.contextbridge.ai). We only run on repos you select, our agents run in a short-lived microVM per run, we use Amazon Bedrock with zero-data-retention, and never train on your code. We're offering 25 free PRs per GitHub org, per month with no credit card required. Additional PRs are billed at about $1/PR, with discounts for higher volume. We also would love to accelerate OSS projects, so reach out to ask about additional free credits. If you hate dealing with Dependabot PRs, we'd love for you to give it a shot and tell us what you think. Josh, Donnie, and I will be around answering any questions and responding to any feedback you have.

leads.title: Wiki-driven development: coding agents update a wiki for you, you set direction
leads.description: My team has been working in a way we are calling calling wiki-driven development, where the wiki is written for the human, not the agent and the human uses primarily the wiki to set direction for the agent. This is different from Karparthy's LLm I'm curious whether others do something like it. Once I run several coding agents at a time, I get overwhelmed and disorganized. Every session makes decisions and raises questions, and I can't reread the transcripts. CLAUDE.md and agent memory help the agent, but they don't give me a place to see what is going on and decide. The problem gets worse with a team. So, I have the agents write a wiki, and they write it for me. As they work, they record only what is significant: decisions with who made them, when, and the option we passed over; open questions with an owner; and a short summary of where each area stands. I ask it to focus on the big picture, strategy, key architectural or business decisions. In more detail: 1. Agents do the work and update the pages it affects with what is significant: key decisions, key strategic points, open questions, and a summary of where things stand. 2. I read the wiki to understand the big picture: the key points, where we are, and what still needs to be decided. It is short enough to read. 3. I think and decide there: I settle a question, change a decision, lay out some more strategy points, or rewrite a page to say where I want to go. 4. The next session builds from the page I changed. Karpathy's LLM Wiki idea is related, but it compiles sources you collect into a knowledge base that keeps getting richer. His goal is completeness for research. Our approach is minimalistic: the pages distill way down from the agents' sessions, hold only what is significant, and exist only so I can think and decide. Spec-driven development has you write the spec up front for the agent to implement. Here the agent writes the wiki based on all the valuable detail that are in my session prompts and its response and I edit the wiki, so the document keeps up with the agents work and my job is thinking, organizing, deciding, direction. Here are some things I have learned doing this: - Organization is key for me as the human. I make the agent make a nice visual html with clickable links marketecture or architecture or business model canvas as the top page and navigate from there. I have it keep each page a page long so I actually am motivated to read stuff. - Have the decisions record the rejected options, so when someone brings a question back, the reasoning is available. We are constantly revisiting decisions as we work and learn and so this is very helpful. - The agent wants to write everything down. The criteria I give it is to only record what it would need to get back to where we are right now in terms of strategy, decisions, implementation. Its not that much. You can do the same with a CLAUDE.md that tells the agent what to record, and work in markdown files or Obsidian or Notion. We got so into this that we turned it into a free, MIT-licensed plugin for Claude Code and Codex that keeps the wiki as markdown files in your repo and lets you see the wiki in your browser locally: https://github.com/nimbalyst/nimbalyst-wiki. Do you work in this way? If so, what other things should we be doing and how have you made it work well?

leads.title: Show HN: Gauge – Open-Source CLI to recursively improve your docs
leads.description: Hi HN, I’m Evan from Gauge. We’re open-sourcing our CLI to recursively improve your docs for coding agents. The CLI includes a local execution backend, so you don't need an account to try it. Explainer video here: https://youtu.be/zhLUlIKB1Mg The CLI supports a hillclimbing loop: - set up tasks for coding agents that would need your docs, like 'set up Gauge CI checks' - run the tasks - analyze session transcripts for friction or failures - create variants of your docs to resolve the issues - re-run the tasks with the doc variants injected (transparently, at the same hostname) - repeat until you have a variant that resolves the issues The same loop supports hillclimbing your Skills, CLI, and other agent-facing surfaces. We started out 2 years ago building open-source developer tools (like Tach https://github.com/tach-org/tach ), then pivoted to AI Search optimization, and are now focused on the intersection of the two spaces. We were already working with awesome devtool companies, and they were the first ones to ask us how to optimize for Claude Code and Codex. We realized this would be something that eventually every company needs to do. Our CLI provides primitives for docs/devrel/eng teams to measure, analyze, and improve how coding agents use their product. The design boils down to two components: VMs and a network gateway. The VMs are straightforward, we want the agents to be highly privileged within their environment so that they are representative of developers' coding agents. Each VM generally comes with the agent harness itself, language toolchains, and a git repository. The network gateway is where we terminate TLS and swap in variants of your docs transparently. The gateway also handles credential replacement, so agents see placeholders and can't exfiltrate keys. The CLI comes with a 'local' execution backend (inference is still remote). For VMs, it uses Docker containers, and the network gateway is mitmproxy running in a sidecar container for each session. We've used the hillclimbing loop internally to find and fix coding agent issues like mistaken pricing, inaccurate product limitations, and repeated workarounds. We saw coding agents report that Gauge only supports Claude Code and Codex, traced it back to the web pages they fetched, and fixed the behavior (we support Pi, OpenCode, and Antigravity as well). For Clerk, we helped shift coding agents from their legacy 'keyless' mode to their new 'clerk init' command. They were able to validate a pre-release change to their SDK's error messages using Gauge, then saw a 3x increase in coding agents using 'clerk init' post-deploy. Due to the 'static' nature of AI models, we've realized that closed-loop optimization techniques are now possible for essentially all software products. The same agent can be simulated over and over, meaning that a high-fidelity testing environment is all you need. Achieving the best results boils down to high-quality analysis (finding generalizable friction and objections) and paired experiments (vary only the content, measure the downstream change in behavior). The repo is here: https://github.com/gauge-sh/gauge-cli and you can start using the CLI with: npm i -g @withgauge/cli We also have documentation and a quickstart here: https://docs.withgauge.com/agents/guides/cli If you point a coding agent at those pages, it should guide you through the initial setup - let us know if it doesn't! The intention is for your agent to run some sensible evaluations and find at least one point of friction you can fix. We'd love to know from HN: Has anyone tried to DIY this locally, or built something in-house at their company? Is this an improvement? If not, what would need to change?

leads.title: Show HN: Globalize.now – translations that land in your pull request
leads.description: Hi HN, I'm Arturs, cofounder of globalize.now. Our view is that the best developer tools don't ask teams to change how they work. They show up where the work already happens. Dependabot doesn't make you log into a dependency dashboard; it opens a PR. Localization mostly works the other way. A TMS brings its own dashboard, upload and download loops, review queues, and a sync step someone has to own. Liam and I spent years at Lokalise watching teams reshape their process around that. It fits a localization department. It doesn't fit a small team shipping daily. So we built translation into the PR itself. Connect your GitHub repo, open a PR as usual, and we translate the new or changed strings, run QA checks, and commit the locale files to that same PR. The feature and its translations get reviewed and merged together, so nothing ships half-translated. If you'd rather keep translations separate, pick a branch instead: every push to it gets its own translation PR. Either way, files stay in your repo in your library's own format, so there's nothing to sync and nothing to migrate off. This can look trivial. A GitHub Action that sends changed strings to an LLM is an afternoon's work, and plenty of you have built one. The afternoon version is where it starts, though. Keeping terminology consistent, not re-translating what hasn't changed, catching broken placeholders and plural forms, and not paying for the whole catalog on every push is the part that keeps needing attention. We'd rather own that so you don't have to. Glossaries, style guides and translation memory are built in, and they push the output toward what a good localization team would produce. We run it on our own site, which is mostly long-form content (blog posts). Adding Japanese and Brazilian Portuguese (about 5,600 strings each) took 8 minutes and cost €31. If your app isn't i18n-ready yet, an agent skill sets up the library, extracts hardcoded strings and connects the repo: npx skills add globalize-now/globalize-skills Pricing starts at €5/month plus usage ~€0.15/1000 chars depending on size of glossary, style guide etc. No seats. We think this "tool in the middle" pattern applies well beyond translation (e.g. accessibility fixes, docs drift, language consistency). We'd like to hear where you think it breaks down, and how it works for you in practice. Try it at https://globalize.now .

leads.title: Show HN: 8 years of "Who's Hiring?" in charts (hiring boom, bust, and AI trends)
leads.description: After seeing Andrej's HackerTube post (and given my sons are both junior-mid developers) I decided to point Codex at 8 years of "Who's hiring?" posts and rip through some tokens on semantic analysis of all that content. I started pre-COVID, thru October 2026, and the data was retrieved via HN API data. 5 things that stand out: 1. AI is now in half the posts. AI or machine learning appeared in 50% of 2026 posts, up from 17% in 2019. 2. Most employers posted in only one month. Across all 94 monthly threads, 53% of the employers we identified appeared in just one month. 3. Frontend roles fell from 16% to 3% of posts. That’s a substantial shift in the kinds of developers companies explicitly say they’re looking for. 4. Staff-level posts grew 3.6×. Posts naming staff-level roles rose from 77 in 2019 to 277 in 2026, even as the hiring board got smaller. 5. Only 41 posts explicitly named junior roles in 2026. Out of 2,932 posts. In 2019, there were 163. ... plus 20 other trends. It feels like there's plenty to consider and discuss. Hope it's useful.

leads.title: Show HN: A terminal viewer for plain text data files (JSON,YAML,CSV,XML,)
leads.description: When I started working hands-on with OpenAPI specifications, it became clear very quickly that using an editor to read large volumes of deeply nested JSON sucks, a very great deal. So I went looking for something to help, and came across https://jless.io This is an awesome terminal app for navigating nasty JSON documents. I am forever indebted to Paul Martinez for writing this tool. But it did have some gaps. It couldn't reload files that had changed, keeping your place in the JSON structure, which I really needed. And it only loaded one file at a time. But unfortunately it was written in Rust, and I didn't know Rust, and back in the pre-AI days that was kind of a huge blocker. But of course once we got models that could actually write decent code, the obvious idea came to me - I'll just add my features and submit a PR! Happy days. Except by that stage my requirements had grown - I also needed to handle many other file formats, like CSV, TOML, INI, and even XML. So I got side-tracked extending another side-project - an easy going JSON parser that supported comments, and trailing commas, the usual sort of thing. During COVID, with a SaaS startup in the events space now on the rocks, I was looking for some distraction and decided to refactor this little easy-going JSON parser of mine. It used a generated parser and was slow. I read some blog posts about how all production-grade language parsers are pretty much hand-crafted recursive descent, and thought, how hard could it be! Five years later, after many many fun experiments, and production use, I ended up with a runtime parser system: https://tabnas.dev This is a quirky approach to parsing that is partly recursive descent, partly a state machine, and mostly empirical hacking. It works, and it's pretty fast, and I use it for real projects. It has the nice property that grammars are dynamic - you don't generate code, the grammar is executed. A fancy regular expression engine, but revved up to parse anything into a proper abstract syntax tree. Now with that in hand, I could return to the original project and create my own version of jless that solved the itches I needed to scratch: a watch mode; multiple tabs; load any data format into a tree structure Now I still don't know Rust. I mean I like the idea, but there are only so many hours in the day. But now we have AI, so now I do get to go to the candy store. Combining jless.io, and tabnas.dev, and my requirements, I built (caused to be built?), aless - the less for any format! Now this is also a nice stress test for the tabnas parsing engine, and I was very pleased about that too. So if you need to review lots of data structure files on the command line, and need a terminal app to do so, this is for you. I can't help but be struck by the irony however that the need for such a thing is much less now - I mostly get agents to look at large JSON documents now. Still, our puny human brains need help sometimes, and this lets me review documents when I need to. It is also really nice and satisfying to see how easy it is to now bring together open source components to create what is essentially personal software. But I think the key thing out of this little project is that the basic physics of software development remain the same. Software should be built from components glued together. Components should have well-defined interfaces. Aim to reduce cognitive load - this is useful to both humans and machines. Yes, the entire thing could be built from scratch, using a textual specification, and be a mire of over-engineered AI slop, and still be perfectly usable. But the way I actually built it, with AI as a coding companion, using components was deeply satisfying because I still understand the essence of the code, while being able to ignore the accidental complexity. Components give you another layer of abstraction with fewer things to think about, and that allows your human mind to sta

leads.description: Guys - OpenAI Decisions, Jev, World Models are interesting. We ran some tests for the C-suite to decide between OpenAI Decisions vs. their own existing models vs. training their proprietary Financial World Model. Sharing the results of our sample tests. Which involves which business cases, they wish to map on which Decision models. Summary: Small Financial World Model compared to OpenAI Decisions. This test is not to build a better model. But to help C-suites make informed choices. There are various considerations viz Latency Cost per decision On-premises or Hosted APIs Regulatory & Compliance Mapping to use cases Financial modelling or LLM-based reasoning as underlying architecture We ran tests to: Predict credit defaults Cross-sell propensity Churn Risk Future cash flows Future state of customers & causal impacts of interventions like no-action, Payment reminders etc. These tests are specific to banking use cases. Why Benchmark & comparison: Small on-prem Decision Models are needed due to latency, cost, regulatory or protecting the proprietary data for Enterprises. This benchmarking helps C-suite executives to decide which option - their in-house models or other options are better. Vaayu FinBench also includes some specific banking-related business cases as examples. World Model also has action-conditioning. Thus, it predicts which decision optimizes the future outcomes. Eg Risk weighted return or prevent default. Core ask from Banks Small Financial World Model is trained on-premesis on proprietary data for enterprises. Scope - This is only for demonstration purposes to give a glimpse of how to compare various options. The dataset & model size is way too small yet. On a larger proprietary dataset, the results need to be benchmarked. Results: Latency - A co-located Small Financial World Model way improves latency. Major part may be coming due to network latency. leads.title: Show HN: Korosta – Remember and highlight job postings you've seen
leads.description: # What is and whats not Korosta is a privacy-first user-customizable tool to highlight job postings based on how frequent are those, and your ratings: * how often the job postings appeared to the user -> fade repeatedly seen job postings * learns from your ratings with a simple local model -> highlight relevant ones * 2 versions: free and pro * almost everything is kept local (ratings, recipes, customizations, history), only licensing and payments require a server * no account required to use it (just when doing the purchase) This is not a job tracker, job board, or automated application system. It just annotates what you already have visible in your browser's tab. ## Links chrome: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/korosta/dhpnogbefak... firefox: https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/korosta/ Howto create recipes fast (With the help of a LLM): https://covatools.com/korosta/howtos/create-cookbook-with-an... Website (with ultra short videos): https://korosta.app # Why This idea started like 2 years ago, when I was laid off from a tech company (2024's common rounds), and I started the stressful job searching. For job searching, my main platform was, and still is, linkedin: I perfected my url parameters so I can easily have my 10 different tabs. But one questions that commonly had, was "Have I already seen this job post?", and honestly, I wont be saving manually every item in a tool like trello (or the new ones). That question plus my bad memory had me with: "that role is awesome!!! ohhh I already seen it... but 2 months ago" (something like job posting recycling? maybe). The main objective of this tool/extension is to reduce the load / fatigue of remembering what you have already seen (and not in just a single site), and also highlight what could be interesting to you personally (by learning with your ratings) -> less time searching, and thus, giving more time to apply in the relevant ones, or doing something else (like recovering your energy). One thing I also spent time around was in the customization / editor (+ the howto in the page), so almost anybody can extend the tool (recipes/cookbook) <- I get frustrated when I love a tool but I fully depend on the developer # beyond the technical part (more context... you can skip it, and test already) Around 16.5 years ago I wanted to develop and sell apps, like the trend in those days... I did not. One year ago, I was thinking the same with the first version, the tool was working (even though over engineered), but I got discouraged by myself by reading all the terms of services, legal + fiscal topics, all the things that I did not know... plus some sites are very aggressive with their terms of use and tools like this. I got a job, then changed my career path to a contractor, and meanwhile I started looking for a job again, but since the end of 2025 I really understand the new difficulties of the job market + not being sooo young, so I took the previous tool, refurbished it but with a different mindset: customization first with a simple learning algorithm so it can highlight interesting jobs to the user -> the name of the tool "Korosta" means highlight in Finnish (its difficult to find a good name ha). I do think that is even more relevant to release it now because of AI: some platforms are pushing heavily their AI-based search engines, that are not so easy yet to customize -> putting more stress / burden on us. In terms of monetization, I defined it based on: I am not keen of subscriptions, I grew up with shareware (like Doom... you can guess my age now), and when a single payment give you something (I wont distribute this in floppies, though). And it ended like: pay once and keep for the same major version. I learned a lot, and I am still learning, with this development, so I want to hear you
